speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: TABLING OF PROPOSALS AND REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table, in both official languages, a copy of the government's proposals to correct certain anomalies, inconsistencies, certain archaisms and errors, and to deal with other matters of a non-controversial and uncomplicated nature in the Statutes of Canada.
There have been consultations among the parties and I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that there is the traditional unanimous consent to refer this draft bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF PROPOSALS AND REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in giving the unanimous consent of the opposition to this matter, I would like to make one brief point, if I may.
A number of the amendments contained within the bill are amendments which have come to the House from the Joint Standing Committee on Scrutiny of Regulations. I was a former chairman of that committee, and it is my hope that the government will consider enlarging the criteria that are used in agglomerating amendments inside that bill.
I consider it a very useful device for achieving necessary changes in the laws of Canada of a non-controversial nature and also reflecting legal advice and second thoughts about certain clauses of the legislation. I have always regretted that the miscellaneous amending process is not used more openly and more generously than it is.
I am offering my consent to seeing this bill referred. I think it is a very useful decision. I am looking forward to the work of the committee.
I hope that the government will review, and I regret not seeing the minister nodding, but I hope he will at least think about a process to be developed whereby more advice can be taken more directly from this all-party committee, which is usually unanimous and which makes recommendations for amendments which sometimes take years instead of months to find their way into miscellaneous amending packages.

subsubtopic: TABLING OF PROPOSALS AND REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise just briefly to indicate that certainly we agree with this process. This is the traditional method of proceeding with these amendments.
I wish to urge the government to continue a process which it started in this miscellaneous statutes amendments process, that is, to ensure that all statutes in Canada use non-sexist language. This is an area in which the government has been moving, but there are certainly far too many statutes which reflect sexist language. Hopefully, this process of statutory amendment is one of the means that can be used to make those important changes.

Mr. Speaker, under Statements by Ministers, I want to ask the government House Leader a question.
This is the twenty-fifth anniversary of our flag, a flag of which we are all proud, a flag which represents the compassionate tolerance, political, social, religious and economic freedoms that we have come to enjoy in our country.
I would assume that someone from the government would want to speak on this today, recognizing that during the flag debate itself there were 180 speeches against the flag given by Conservative members over a seven-month period. After 180 speeches, most of which were 40 minutes in duration, the government of the day brought in closure to end what was obviously months and months of debate against the flag.
I assume with that interest in the flag, some minister would want to say something about that final vote, particularly in light of the fact that it took seven months of debate before we got to that point.

want to do that, but we did not want to do it before the hon. member for Chambly had a chance to give his comments.

I feel, as does my friend from the New Democratic Party, that we are witnessing something of a rewrite of history when we consider the enthusiasm with which the entire House greeted the flag 25 years ago in a way which does not correspond with today's reality.
However, no one is more proud of the flag today than the Conservative party and its members, and no one is more proud than the Liberals and the New Democrats. I think those of us who track the Conservative party should recognize that they eventually bring themselves on to the right side of history.

I rise to ask you to review the rules governing the presentation of the budget and consider whether or not those rules provide for a 10-minute question and comment period to follow the delivery of the budget in the House by the Minister of Finance.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House, a few brief rulings done on previous occasions regarding the questions and comments, in hopes that you would find it is the clear intention of the House that such a
Routine Proceedings
question and comment period be held when the relevant Standing Orders were adopted.
Standing Order 84(7), governs time limits and comments on speeches during the budget debate. It states:
No Member, except the Minister of Finance, the Member speaking first on behalf of the Opposition, the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, shall speak for more than twenty minutes at a time in the Budget debate. Following the speech of each Member a period not exceeding ten minutes shall be made available, if required, to allow Members to ask questions and comment briefly on matters relevant to the speech and to allow responses thereto.
The wording of this Standing Order is virtually identical to that of Standing Order 50(2), which governs another special debate in the House, the Address in Response to the Speech from the Throne.
In considering then whether there can be questions and comments following the Budget speech, it is quite pertinent to look to rulings regarding the nearly identically worded provisions for the Address and Reply.
For example, on December 9,1983, the then Leader of the Opposition, who is currently the Prime Minister, replied to the Throne Speech. speechtext:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-38 be amended in Clause 23
(a)	by striking out line 22 at page 16 and substituting the following therefor:
"within thirty days after the claim arose,"
(b)	by striking out lines 33 to 35 at page 16 and substituting the following therefor:
"opinion that to bar the proceed-"
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-38 be amended by deleting Clause 23.
He said, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could start out by saying that I was a member of the legislative committee that studied this bill. I want to say that I thought the committee was conducted by the government members on it, as well as the chairman, in a way that was very fair. In moving this amendment, I am not seeking to do so in a particularly partisan way because I recognize the government agreed to many worth while amendments to this bill. I felt that all the members of the committee co-operated very well to do the best they could to make this bill a better bill than it was when it left this House at second reading, and I think there have been some significant improvements.
However, one of the improvements that did not get made was the one to Section 23 of the bill which is a relatively minor but still an important item in the bill. Perhaps it would be clearer for Your Honour if I read Section 23 which amends Section 12 of the Crown Liability Act. The section states:
"12. (1) No proceedings lie against the Crown by virtue of Paragraph 3(b) unless, within seven days after the claim arose, notice in writing of the claim and of the injury complained of has been served on a responsible official of the department or agency administering the
February 15, 1990

property or the employee of the department or agency who is in control or charge of the property.
My objection to the current wording is the requirement that seven days' notice of claim be given. Part of the purpose of the act was to treat the Crown more as an ordinary person. No other individual or corporation in Canada, and I am using the word "person" here in its legal sense, is subject to this kind of protection.
For example, if a person is driving along a road owned by the federal Crown in the Northwest Territories and his car falls into a large hole caused by excavation by the federal Crown employees maintaining the road, that person would have to give notice within seven days after the claim arose of the injury complained of, or he might find that his claim is out of time, in other words, that there was a bar to his proceeding on that claim.
In my view, no other "person", no other corporation has such protection. If CPR happened to own a road somewhere in Canada and somebody drove into a hole on its road, no seven day notice requirement is there. The lawsuit could commence in the usual course of things within six years after the claim arose. Therefore, there is a a six-year limitation period that applies to CP, that applies to me, any member in this House, or any individual in Canada where the Crown has this special deal of seven days.
The parliamentary secretary, who I presume will be answering for the Minister of Justice in this matter, will say: "Well yes, but you must read subsection 2," which states:
(2) Failure to give, or insufficiency of, the notice required by subsection (1) is not a bar to the proceedings if the court in which the proceedings are taken is of the opinion that the Crown in its defence was not prejudiced by the want or insufficiency of the notice and that to bar the proceedings would be an injustice, notwithstanding that reasonable excuse for the want or insufficiency of the notice is not established.
There are two proposed amendments, as Your Honour has indicated.
The first one is to change the seven day period to thirty, which is not much of a concession but it is some. I invite the parliamentary secretary to consider that.
The second amendment would be to take out the provision in subsection (2) that would require the plaintiff in an action to show that the Crown was not prejudiced by the want or insufficiency of the notice. In
Government Orders
other words, the question of prejudice to the Crown is not the issue. The question really is would it be an injustice to prevent the plaintiff from proceeding with his claim, and only that issue, not the question of whether the Crown was prejudiced by the notice. Because if the Crown states that it has nobody around who can say whether or not there was a hole in that road on that day, the Crown is going to say it is prejudiced because its witness is dead, its people have left the area, or there is no one who worked in that area left in its employ and it cannot find them.
It seems to me that that ought not to be the test, because that defence is not available to anyone else. Although in the case of individuals, it maybe possible for an individual to remember a hole in his driveway on a particular day, it will not be for a large corporation and why should the Crown be placed in a better position than a large corporation?
I have put that amendment as one of my amendments. The second amendment is to get rid of the clause entirely. I invite the minister to consider that possibility. If he really wanted to treat the Crown as an ordinary citizen in this instance, and I invite him to do so, he could simply delete the entire clause. If that is unacceptable, then I would request that he consider the other amendments I have proposed which would extend the notice period by 30 days and take away the requirement that prejudice to the Crown or non-prejudice to the Crown be shown by a plaintiff before he is allowed to proceed if he has missed the time period specified in the section.
I hope that the parliamentary secretary will consider my remarks in the spirit in which they are intended. They are not intended as a criticism of the bill as drafted. I recognize that this is a relatively standard type of limitation clause protecting Crowns. But I do think in this day and age the Crown in right of Canada, and certainly in right of the provinces, does not need this kind of protection, in my submission.
The answer given in committee when this issue was raised there was that this was exactly what was done in Ontario under the Municipal Act, for example, so why should we not follow the same procedure. What I am saying to the parliamentary secretary is let the House be a leader in this regard and let us start changing some of these archaic rules that, while protecting the Crown,

Government Orders
harm our citizens. They lessen the rights of the citizens of the country. Surely the Crown as a representative of the citizens, as it is coming increasingly to be, and after all Parliament is its representative, ought not to be looking at itself to be protecting itself from its citizens but in fact to help the citizenry. If it is going to give rights to citizens to sue one another or other corporations without a 7,10 or 30-day notice period, surely it does not need to insist on such notice for itself as against its own citizens, which is exactly what Section 23 is doing.
I ask the parliamentary secretary and the minister to consider removing this particular section from the bill altogether and, if that is not acceptable, to agree with my other amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking on Motion No. 1, and indirectly on Motion No. 2,1 would like to echo the comments of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands about the spirit with which the legislative committee approached this bill. Certainly, there were significant improvements to the legislation in a number of areas. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands played a very distinguished role in the Chair. He was certainly veiy vigorous in that role on a number of occasions. I think that we came out with a better bill as a result of that process.
There were a number of areas in which I sought improvements to the legislation by amending the bill, in some cases successfully and in other cases the government defeated those amendments. Clause 23 was one of those clauses in which I did seek an amendment very similar to that which is proposed by the member for Kingston and the Islands. There is absolutely no reason to maintain this seven-day notice provision. I fully support Motion No. 1 which would extend that period to 30 days and which would also make certain changes in the second part of it.
I must say that I am astonished at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that if that fails that we should repeal Clause 23. What the Liberal member is suggesting is that we move backward to the status quo and that the current provisions of Clause 23, although limited, would in fact remove the requirement in the existing subsection 12(1) that a copy of the notice
of claim be sent to the Deputy Attorney General of Canada. In addition, the new Clause 23 would remove the exception in subsection 12(2) concerning the failure or insufficiency of notice.
Clause 23 is a step in the right direction. It does remove a couple of barriers that now exist for the citizen seeking justice before the Federal Court. I am very disappointed at the suggestion of the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands that he wants to go back to the status quo. That is exactly what he would be doing by repealing Clause 23 in its entirety. He would be going back to the existing provisions of the Code.
I do not know whether it is the position of the Liberal Party that these barriers, which now exist in Clause 12 with respect to the notice, and the exceptions remain.
I would call upon the member for Kingston and the Islands to reconsider Motion No. 2 and to recognize that certainly there are improvements that can and should be made to this clause, but in the event that Motion No. 1 is not successful, I would suggest, with respect, to the member for Kingston and the Islands that proceeding with Motion No. 2 would be a step backwards. I am not at all sure that he would want to take that step which would in fact weaken the rights of the citizen in litigation against the Crown.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to echo the comments of my colleagues that this bill is a step in the right direction and that there were significant improvements that were made at the legislative committee. While I always strive, if possible, to agree with a fellow alumni from Queen's University it is not always possible. I notice he is wearing his Queen's crest today on his jacket. I do not know if that was a coincidence, but nonetheless I think
February 15, 1990

that we are going to have to agree to disagree on the two motions that he has proposed to the House on Bill C-38.
I would suggest to the House that a seven-day notice for a proceeding against the Crown is not an unreasonable notice. I wanted to correct an impression that may have been left by the member proposing this, that we were doing so on the basis or our justification was the limitation period within the Ontario Municipal Act. I do remember making the comment and I said I thought it was a 48 hour notice, but regardless I think there is far more to this than the fact that the provinces or the municipalities across this countiy may have a shorter notice period of time.
The member talked about the Crown and the prejudice to individuals. I agree that this bill has gone a long way to putting the Crown on a more equitable footing with those who seek to bring an action against the Crown. But the Crown is not exactly like another individual in this country. The Crown should be equated with the public interest in Canada. The public interest in proceedings against the Crown is, of course, the Canadian taxpayer. I do not think it is unreasonable to ask those who have an action to be brought against the Crown to bring that within seven days.
I can tell the hon. member that, yes, I had a look at that. I had some of the same concerns that he did, that that is a very short limitation period. He anticipated the argument that I would make. There is a saving provision in the second part of that that gives relief to those who bring an action or who give notice to the Crown outside of the seven-day period. The wording is "the relief can be granted if there is no prejudice to the Crown." I think that is reasonable and I have to disagree with him that the only basis for relief is if there is an injustice to the plaintiff. These are proceedings against the Crown, they bind the Canadian taxpayer to pay if there is a successful lawsuit. So I cannot agree that we should remove the clause that protects the Crown nor should we remove the clause that is the saving provision on this.
The hon. member pointed out that if we abolish the clause altogether, and it was quite correctly pointed out by the member for Burnaby-Kingsway, that that would be an intolerable position. The member said that there would be a six-year limitation period under tort law. That is too long for a number of reasons. As you know

Mr. Speaker, the Crown controls and owns millions of acres across this country. If there is an accident on Crown land that gives rise to an action, we should be notified immediately for a number of reasons.
First, it allows the Crown to decide whether an action should go forward. Nobody wants to prolong litigation. Everyone wants to settle litigation as quickly as possible. With a seven-day notice period, the Crown is able to assess what it is that has gone wrong on Crown land and then make a determination as to whether a settlement should be made. That is in the interests of all parties.
As well, and I think the hon. member should have brought this to our attention, if there is something on Crown land that is a danger to the public, the Crown should be notified. That is in the public interest because the Crown wants to correct that situation. To let a hazardous situation continue indefinitely-

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Hon. Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada I have the honour to speak at second reading of Bill C-59, the British Columbia Courts Amendment Act. This act would amend the Judges Act as well as a number of ancillary clauses resulting from the changes in court structures in the province of British Columbia.
The Government of Canada is committed to making the judicial system in Canada more efficient. To that end the federal government is co-operating with the provinces to improve the administration of justice throughout the country.
One example of that is the government's policy of responding positively to the initiatives of provincial governments to reorganize the Provincial Superior District and County Courts to better suit and improve the administration of justice in the provinces.
The amendments contained in Bill C-59 will give effect to the decision of the province of British Columbia to merge its county courts into the British Columbia Supreme Court. Legislation to effect the merger of the County Courts with the Supreme Court of British Columbia was adopted by the province of B.C. in June, 1989, to come into force July 1, 1990 or such earlier date as might be fixed by proclamation.
Bill C-59 would enact the complementary amendments to federal legislation in consequence upon the merger of the courts.
In addition to changing the name of the court where it appears in federal statutes, this legislation will make the changes in the Judges Act necessary to reflect the new
Government Orders
organization of British Columbia's courts, including their creation of a new position of Associate Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
This bill is neither major nor complex. All of its provisions might be described as technical, yet it contributes substantially to the more effective functioning of the legal system in British Columbia by making the necessary amendments to federal statutes to permit the court merger in that province.
In addition, this bill represents another example of this government's commitment to co-operating with the provinces and territories to the benefit of all Canadians. I would ask the support of all members in ensuring speedy passing of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, our party supports the position of the government. We see this legislation as something that should probably happen in B.C., but in part it is up to the people of B.C. to make this decision. I believe there are about seven or eight provinces across the country that now have a unified court system. Obviously for B.C. to move in this direction is a positive statement.
We in New Brunswick went through this process about eight or nine years ago, and there is always some hesitation and concern, particularly among conservative barristers who are reluctant to change and reluctant to go through that process.
If the New Brunswick experience is any indication, the process works well and was an improvement. One is not faced with trying to decide in which court to proceed because there is only one court. We think this is a move in the right direction.
We would urge all those people in British Columbia who have concerns to come before the committee studying the legislation to make sure that their views are heard. We agree with the parliamentary secretary that it is more technical in nature than substantive, but the effects can be substantive. That is why these groups, organizations and individuals should come forward.
Perhaps, once all the courts are unified under one system, we should be considering specialization as far as judges are concerned. That is a choice we may want to look at some time in the future, where you have family law judges, criminal law judges and judges of civil matters.

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
We on this side of the House are supportive of the general direction of this bill and look with interest to the submissions that will be made.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this legislation. As a member of Parliament from the province of British Columbia, I am particularly pleased to note that in effect this proposal of the government would implement legislation that was adopted and supported by all parties in the British Columbia House in June of last year to effect the merger of the county courts with the Supreme Court.
I believe this leaves only one province with split jurisdiction. I believe Nova Scotia retains the split jurisdiction. Hopefully, it too will move under Premier McDonough in the very near future to achieve that important advance.
It has been indicated that the legislation is largely technical in nature, and that is quite accurate. I do want to take this opportunity though, since the subject of this bill is the courts and the merger of the courts, to take a couple of minutes to talk about the important question of access to these courts.
While it is important that we move forward in ensuring the courts are efficient in the administration of justice- and this bill will certainly be a small step in that direction-there are still serious concerns with respect to access to justice in British Columbia in particular but also in other parts of the country.
One of the important elements of justice and access to justice in this land is the ability of those without resources to have access to the courts, whether it be district courts, county courts, the Supreme Court or higher courts. For that reason I want to take this opportunity to express my deep concern and that of my colleagues about the cut-backs in legal aid.
I have the most recent annual report of the Legal Services Society of British Columbia, which is the body responsible for ensuring access to the courts and the provision of legal aid in British Columbia.
In this most recent annual report the chairperson of the board of directors of the Legal Services Society states:
In B.C., legal rights are empty rights. Rights conferred by the
Charter of Rights are rights without remedies because the province
is not providing adequate funding for legal aid services.
Mr. Henderson points out that this is an essential element of a system of justice which is accessible to all citizens. He goes on to point out that some of the particular areas of concern are the low level of tariff paid to lawyers who take on legal aid cases, the absence of adequate resources to provide assistance to people involved in debt litigation, hearings before administrative tribunals in workers' compensation matters, welfare appeals, and refugee claims.
As well, on the question of access the board points out that it is essential that steps be taken to ensure the justice system is responsive to the needs of native people. We have seen a number of inquiries, whether it be the Marshall inquiry in Nova Scotia, the inquiry currently under way in Manitoba or in other jurisdictions which have pointed out serious problems with the accessibility of the justice system to native people in Canada.
The justice reform committee report in British Columbia stated:
Our legal system falls short of providing equal access to all citizens.
I would hope the federal government would accept its responsibility for far more adequate resources to legal aid across this country. I recognize that the federal government does make a significant contribution to legal aid through cost sharing agreements. There is still far more that can be done, and I hope that the government will move in that direction.
On the question of access to justice, particularly under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the minority languages provisions of the Constitution, I want to ask that the Minister of Justice move very quickly to implement the unanimous recommendations of the Standing Committee on Human Rights to fund the Court Challenges Program fully.
This legislation before the House now deals with the efficiency of the courts and an important element of that whole question is the question of access, whether that be through legal aid or through funding under the Court Challenges Program, to make the rights which are on paper a reality to all Canadians.
The unanimous report of the standing committee on the Court Challenges Program pointed out that access to the courts is integral to the effective implementation of constitutional rights. As the Minister of Justice is well aware, this program is struggling. At this point the executive director of the Canadian Council on Social
February 15, 1990

Development has given lay-off notices to the staff of the program. I hope the Minister of Justice in his concern for access to the courts would move veiy quickly to ensure that steps are taken to fund this important program fully.
Finally, I want to take this opportunity to raise concerns on legislation which is largely technical in nature but deals with access to the courts and the efficiency of the court system. Concerns have been raised recently by a number of my colleagues dealing with the whole question of sexism in the courts. This particular legislation deals with courts in British Columbia, but it is not restricted to British Columbia. I regret to say it was a judge in my province who referred to a three year old child as being sexually aggressive.
[ Translation]
Recently, Mr. Speaker, we had a judge in the province of Quebec, Judge Denys Dionne of the Quebec Court in Longueuil, who said in one of his judgments: "As they say, rules are like women: they were made to be violated."
That belies the grim reality of violence directed against women in the country: the fact that a women is raped every 17 minutes in Canada; the fact that one woman in four will be raped some time in her life, most often by someone that she knows; the fact that one in eight girls is sexually assaulted before the age of 18, usually by a male family member; the fact that 54 per cent of women living with men will be struck at some time during the relationship; the fact that 60 per cent of rapes reported and most battering and child sexual assault take place in the home; and, finally, the fact that some 90 per cent of women are sexually harassed on the job at some time in their work life.
I would hope that the minister, in moving forward in this area of improving the efficiency of the courts, would also take steps to ensure that our judges are educated as to the reality of violence against women.
We recall the comments of Madam Justice Bertha Wilson recently and too many other judges: the Quebec judge to whom I have just referred and the Northwest
Government Orders
Territories judge who said sexual assaults are less serious there because most occur when the woman is drunk and passed out and, to quote the judge, "The man comes along, sees a pair of hips and helps himself". There is also the Nova Scotia judge who told women that they should obey their husbands and go back to them.
I would join in the call by many women across Canada and all those concerned about equitable justice for a national task force to examine sex discrimination in the Canadian legal system. I take this opportunity to urge the Minister of Justice to strike a national task force to look into this very serious problem of sexism on the bench.
I just might add that I know there is a recently founded Canadian judicial centre, and I would hope that this centre would play a leading role in helping to educate our judiciary.
There have been more women appointed to the bench recently and certainly the minister is quite accurate in noting that. It is a welcome change from former Conservative governments. Up until 1979 no Conservative government had ever appointed a woman to the bench at any level in the country. We certainly welcome this change as an important step forward.
In conclusion, I support the legislation which is before the House and hope that the government will take note of the concerns I have raised with respect to access to justice in the area of legal aid, the renewal of the Court Challenges Program, and, particularly, the importance of educating our judges about the reality of violence against women in Canadian society.

speakeroldname: Mr. Rob Nicholson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada, I have the honour of speaking at second reading of Bill C-60, the Ontario Courts Amendment Act.
This bill will provide the complementary amendments to the Judges Act and other federal statutes necessary for the implementation of court reform in Ontario.
That province recently enacted legislation to merge the District Court of Ontario with the Superior Trial Court, the High Court of Justice.
The merged court will become the General Division of the Ontario Court of Justice, a comprehensive name to be given to courts of trial jurisdiction in that province. In addition the Court of Appeal, as is the High Court of Justice, a branch of the Supreme Court of Ontario will be constituted as a separate court. The Ontario legislation therefore marks a significant departure from the traditional court structure in that province, virtually untouched since 1881.
The new Ontario Court General Division will be organized on a regional basis. A regional senior judge
will be appointed to administer the court in each of the eight regions under the over-all direction of the chief justice and the associate chief justice of the court.
When the Attorney General of Ontario announced his proposals on May 1, 1989 they were met with varying degrees of acceptance by the legal profession and the public at large. Over the past several months several aspects of these proposals have generated representations to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada from groups and individuals concerned with their effects upon the independence of the judiciary in Ontario.
The hon. minister has therefore been required to take a much closer interest in these proposals than a federal minister would ordinarily accord a province's plans for court structure. On a number of occasions the Minister of Justice has discussed the legislation directly with Mr. Scott. The hon. minister agreed to make a number of changes since incorporated at the committee stage and in an amending bill enacted in December. I think you will find, Mr. Speaker, that these amendments fully meet the concerns which have been expressed.
Bill C-60 itself is largely technical in nature and is designed to reflect in federal statutes changes to the names and structures of Ontario courts. Upon its passage the judges of the existing High Court of Justice and District Court of Ontario will be reappointed to the Ontario Court of Justice General Division, while courts of the present appellate branch of the Supreme Court of Ontario will be reappointed to the separate Court of Appeal.
A number of transitional provisions have been included in this bill. One which I would bring to the attention of hon. members affects the chief judge and the associate chief judge of the District Court of Ontario. On the merger of the High Court of Justice and the District Court, the positions of chief judge and associate chief judge of the District Court will lapse. For reasons of fairness Section 46 of the bill will continue the salary of the chief judge and the associate chief judge at their present level until such time as the salary annexed to the offices they will hold on the new court equals or surpasses it.
Both Chief Judge Lyon and Associate Chief Judge LeSage have occupied their present positions with great distinction for a period of years that would, were it not
February 15, 1990

for the abolition of their court, permit them to take the benefits of Section 32 of the Judges Act.
This section allows a chief justice or chief judge who has served in that capacity for a minimum of five years to step down to a temporary puisne position on the court. By virtue of Subsection 43(2) of the Judges Act, a pension to which a judge would thereafter become entitled will be calculated on the basis of the salary annexed to the office of chief justice or chief judge at the time he or she finally retires or leaves the bench.
In the interest of fairness, subclause 46(2) of this bill will extend the same right to the chief judge and the associate chief judge of the District Court who have held their respective offices for seven years, and in the case of Chief Judge Lyon, for an additional five years as associate chief judge of the court, by deeming them to have made an election under Section 32 of the Judges Act effective upon the merger of the court.
I will note here that it is intended to introduce a number of amendments to this bill in committee to take account of additional purely technical changes required to federal laws. They do not however affect the salient points of Bill C-60.
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the principle of shared jurisdiction as provided under the Constitution, the provinces and the federal government are bound to work together to ensure the proper administration of justice in this country.
An Act of Parliament and decision by the executive authority are necessary to give full effect to the measures being considered by the province with respect to the Constitution of the courts as provided under Section 96 of the Constitution.

Bill C-60, the Ontario Courts Amendment Act, will allow the province of Ontario to institute reforms designed to improve the administration of justice in that province to make the courts more accessible and more responsive to the imperatives of contemporary litigation.
I hope that the spirit motivating these reforms will be accorded the approval of all hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the official opposition I want to welcome the reform of the Ontario system of courts to Parliament.
The relatively modest effort which is before us is really part of a very large parcel of major reform of the court system of the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario is under the leadership of the Attorney General, Ian Scott. This is phase 1 of a two phase project. Phase 1 is already described, discussed and settled. Phase 2 is in the process now of being described. I am looking forward to seeing Parliament play its part in carrying this reform forward.
It should not be surprising, as the earlier discussion revealed, that Nova Scotia, British Columbia and Ontario are the last provinces of our country to be looking to reorganization with a view to greater efficiency of their court system.
I recall from my days of reading history the difficulties that the Fathers of Confederation faced in trying to bring this country together. We have talked in this House very often, and will be talking again this afternoon, about the problems that relate to our language issue, the English and the French.
The resolution of those problems by the Fathers of Confederation was relatively easy compared to the problems that they faced in trying to bring together the original colonies that formed Canada as each had, for long periods of time, an already mature system of justice and courts somewhat similar, but none of them wanting to yield anything to the establishment of the new country of Canada which emerged from the work of the Fathers of Confederation in 1867.
The pressure to maintain the prerogatives of the then existing system were a heavier burden on the Fathers of Confederation than the problems of accommodating English and French within the new country. We see that even today the challenge of modernizing the court systems with a view to greater efficiency and greater comprehensibility by the people of the province is still a task that causes a lot of concern.
I am looking forward to seeing the bill go to committee following second reading. I hope there will be briefs put forward by the various interest groups that are affected, which groups I want to talk about in a moment. I hope we will have some hearings because I do not agree with the government that, as was indicated by the parliamentary secretary, our role is derivative or-he did not use the words "rubber stamp", but he gave the clear impression

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
that our responsibility in this place is to rubber stamp what the provinces have decided to do.
I think we should try to be true to the vision of the Fathers of Confederation in 1867 who wanted to see something of a national system of justice emerge from their work. We must make sure that we do our job and that here in the Parliament of Canada we make a contribution to the work.
In saying that, I think we have also to recognize that a tremendous amount has been done and that the problems and the conflicting and competing interests within the justice system have been addressed by the attorney general. He had numerous meetings with all concerned.
I ought also to pay tribute to Mr. Justice Zuber and to the enormous effort that went into his report which forced the entire community involved in the justice system in the province of Ontario to think again about the system they were living with and about the improvements that could be possible.
Certainly efficiency and comprehensibility were not objectives of the Fathers of Confederation when the system was put together. In those days it was just a matter of trying to get approval and support for Confederation. We began with a system of justice, if one can call it that, which really has no central management. It depends on the working together of four systems, each of which has by tradition, by law, by our Constitution, certain prerogatives and a certain independence.
We are all very aware of the independence of the judiciary, an independence which the system of justice, before its reorganization and when we are finished with its reorganization, must continue. Otherwise, the democracy of Canada will have lost something.
Second, the Crown attorneys have by tradition, by law, certain recognized prerogatives which also have to be accommodated within this so-called system. There is the bar which represents the public, the litigants who come to court to defend themselves, to make claims against fellow citizens, against the government and so on. The whole prerogative that the bar has enjoyed for decades and is a hallmark of our system needs also to be
accommodated within the system which is before us to revise.
Finally, and by no means least important, there is the court system of Ontario which administers the system; the officials, the people who build and manage the court houses with their timetables, the process servers and the paper handlers within the system, all of whom have a responsibility to represent the taxpayers of the province with a system that is efficient and modem and in which things happen and are understood.
Those competing interests, all of which need to be accommodated by the new system, have been broadly involved and are very aware of the implications of the system before us which we are being asked to consider, to look at in committee and to validate by the legislation that the minister has introduced.
I am looking forward very much to our work. The court system faces challenges today that could not even have been dreamed of back in 1867. The fact that the four independent systems have been able to work together and make a system, even though it needs the changes we are considering, is one that we are very proud of. It is a tribute not so much to the structure as to the people who have worked within it, who have recognized each other's role, each other's need for independence, and have done their best to accommodate that. I think it is appropriate to pay tribute to them.
It is taking nothing away from any of them or the role they have played in making the system work so far, to recognize, as seven other provinces have done, including Quebec which has done so from Confederation, that a unified system has considerable advantages.
When I was discussing this bill with some of my colleagues in my caucus who are not members of the bar, they were all delighted to hear, for themselves and on behalf of constituents, that there was going to be a system which would be more comprehensible to them. When the Supreme Court has done something, they will understand more clearly what that means.
At this time we have a Charter, which we did not have, we have a legal aid system, which we did not have, and we have complicated family relations which, more often than they should and certainly more often than in the past, bring members of families to court. We have had a tremendous population growth and one which is very
February 15, 1990

uneven. Some parts of our province have huge populations, others have grown much more slowly, and all of that has had to be accommodated within a system designed in 1867 and revised in a very significant and important way in 1881 and 1882, but really not in any significant way since then.
So I congratulate my colleagues and counterparts in the province of Ontario for the work they have done. I congratulate the Attorney General, Ian Scott, for bringing forward this major initiative, and the Minister of Justice across the floor and his parliamentary secretary for giving us the opportunity now to deal with this bill and to see it carried to committee.
I noted in reading the papers from the process at Queen's Park that it was the hope of the Attorney General that this reform and unification might be in effect by January 1990. That would have been okay with us in the Official Opposition, but it was not presented for second reading until today, which is already after January 1, 1990. I regret that, for whatever reason, the package did not reach us in time to meet the Attorney General's desired target of January 1, 1990, but I hope that we can still make this happen very soon, certainly before the end of 1990, if not months and months before that.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to rise very briefly to indicate that we in the New Democratic Party do indeed support this legislation. Many of the arguments that I made with respect to the preceding bill, the bill that would effect the merger of courts in British Columbia, apply of course to this legislation as well. They include the comments I made with respect to access to the justice system, the funding of legal aid programs and the concerns about the importance of educating the judiciary with respect to sexism in our society and, unfortunately, on the bench.

Mr. Speaker, I also mentioned that extending the Court Challenges Program was important in order to promote access to justice across Canada.
In fact, extending the program is important, not only for equality rights but also and above all for the purpose of promoting and defending the rights of language minorities in this country.
Mr. Speaker, the Court Challenges Program has been in existence since 1978 for cases involving official languages. The fund for this program was established because the government at the time, and in fact all members of Parliament, thought it was important to obtain a court ruling that would specify to what extent the Constitution protects official language minorities.

Mr. Speaker, in 1982, when the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms came into force, the federal government decided to provide for a renewed and expanded program that would finance court challenges by Canada's language minorities.
Mr. Speaker, this program is an important tool for promoting official languages and language rights in this country.
Mr. Speaker, since 1978, the program has funded a number of challenges in our major courts. For instance, the right to be educated in the minority language, as stated in section 23 of the Charter, was the subject of most of the challenges funded by the program.
Last December, the Standing Committee on Human Rights unanimously recommended that the government renew and even expand the Court Challenges Program, both with respect to equality rights and language rights.
I therefore want to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lewis), since we are talking about the courts in Ontario and especially, Mr. Speaker, in recognition of the fact that there are more than one million Francophones in the province of Ontario, to respond-

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak for only a few minutes on this bill. I want to do so from the perspective of a non-lawyer to express to you and to other members of this House just how hopelessly complicated the existing system was and is.
Perhaps to people who are learned in the law it is simple to understand that in the Supreme Court of Ontario there is a Court of Appeal, a High Court of Justice, a District Court, a Surrogate Court, a Unified Family Court, the court Masters and the family law commissioners. Maybe that makes a whole lot of sense to the people in the legal profession, but to the rest of us this is very complicated. For our constituents, those whom we are charged to represent in this House and those whom our colleagues represent in the legislative

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
assembly of our province, it is certainly high time that we make this system a little bit easier to understand.
The bill proposes to do so in two steps. This is not the first attempt at simplifying the court system. It seemed that for the three and a half years that I sat in the Ontario legislature every time we talked about the courts of justice in the Ontario House, it was always for the purpose of making it simpler to understand. It never did get much simpler.
To add to the existing structures I talked about only a moment ago, in the provincial court of Ontario, as opposed to the Supreme Court of Ontario which should be distinguished from the Supreme Court of Canada which we have not talked about, there is the family division, the criminal division and the civil division. Imagine the average Canadian trying to figure out how all of this is supposed to work.
We know that the ultimate objective is to have only two structures, the Court of Appeal and the Ontario Court of Justice. It would seem to me that that would be so much easier to understand and to explain to those we are representing. The old adage that justice delayed is justice denied is not only true. Using the same analogy, you could debate whether justice that is not understandable to the average person is justice at all when it is beyond reach and comprehension of so many people because it is so hopelessly complicated.
To add to this very complicated structure, we have all the tribunals and quasi-judicial organizations that exist both provincially and federally. I think, for instance, at the federal level of such organizations as the Immigration Appeal Board, which is very structured. The justices, if that is what they call themselves, or panel members, walk into the room and everyone is expected to rise as if you were appearing before the Supreme Court. There are other organizations which are a lot less formal. However, as far as I am concerned, those boards and tribunals act in a way which is far too formal.
I know that some people would say that some of them should be changed into courts. I happen to disagree with that proposition. I think there is a need for these quasi-judicial bodies to operate in a less formal manner so that the average constituent can go there with his friend or neighbour and express his point of view.
I do not want to take much more time. I recognize that we want this bill to proceed today. I think you will hear in a few moments of the co-operation that our party is willing to provide in order to enable that to proceed.

I therefore want to congratulate the Attorney General of Ontario on this excellent initiative. It was high time something was done in this respect, and I am very pleased to see this kind of co-operation between the federal government and the province. I think the Liberal minister from Ontario is to be commended for his progressive attitude and his desire to make the justice system more accessible to Canadians.

Of course I want to offer as well my good wishes to the minister across who has co-operated with the provincial Liberal minister who has all the foresight. I am glad that the federal Minister of Justice took heed of the foresight of his provincial Liberal counterpart.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
that Bill C-53, an act to amend the Criminal Code (arson), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on a subject of concern to many Canadians. I think all of us know what a terrible destructive force fire can be when it occurs. Fires cause death, injury and property damage every day in this country. Most are the result of accident or carelessness, but some are deliberately, recklessly or negligently caused by someone. This was the case in over 10,500 fires in 1988. This was a 17 per cent increase over 1987.
Arson is a major crime in Canada and statistics illustrate its seriousness. Arson accounts directly for at least 13 per cent of all reported fires. In 1988 arson was the cause of 42 deaths and injuries to 456 civilians and fire-fighters, many of the latter being volunteers. In the same year the value of insurable losses caused by arson and other set fires was more than $198 million. The
Government Orders
actual economic loss is estimated to be four to five times that amount.
In Canada many of the original arson provisions of the Criminal Code have not been amended substantially since the Code was implemented in 1892. The present provisions are contained in Part 11 of the Code which deals with criminal acts with respect to certain property. Sections 433 to 436 provide for several offences of arson including setting a fire by negligence. As well, they contain a presumption of fraudulent intent on the part of a beneficiary of an insurance policy.
The present law on arson focuses on property. A distinction is drawn as to the types of property that are covered by the crime of arson. However, Bill C-53 focuses on the danger that fire poses to the life, health, safety and property of all Canadians, and particularly to fire-fighters.

Since 1975, the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs, the Association of Canadian Fire Marshals and Fire Commissioners, and the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police have repeatedly called for amendments to the Criminal Code provisions respecting arson.
The resolutions adopted at their annual meetings recommend that the scope of the crime of arson be extended to cover all property, that explosion be included as means to commit arson and that possession of an incendiary material in suspicious circumstances be made a crime.
In 1975, the Uniform Law Conference passed similar resolutions and recommended that the Department of Justice review the sections of the Criminal Code dealing with arson.

In 1984 the Law Reform Commission of Canada published its Working Paper 36 on arson. It stated that the law is both archaic and inadequate. It made five recommendations which called for significant simplification of the law. Following publication of that working paper the Department of Justice studied the Law Reform Commission's recommendations as well as the proposals of various concerned groups. Consultations were also carried out with representatives of the prosecution and defence bars, law professors, the police, fire

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
chiefs, fire marshals and the fire insurance industry. The present bill incorporates many of the recommendations which were voiced in these consultations.
I am not going to go into a great amount of detail but there are some points that I want to make with respect to the bill. First, there is the modernization of the definition of the crime; second, the reformulation of the crime of negligent arson; third, the reformulation of the present presumption in Sections 435 and 436; and fourth, the creation of a new offence of possession of incendiary materials.
At present arson is defined as wilfully setting fire to specific types of property. The Law Reform Commission proposed to redefine arson as any conduct which causes an explosion or a fire which results in the destruction of or damage to property. We have adopted virtually all of these elements in the definition of the offence of arson. First, explosion as well as a fire is a means of committing the offence. Second, damage to property is a necessary element of the defence. Third, the distinctions which exist in the present law as to types of property which may be the subject of an arson are eliminated.
I want to address these changes.
It is increasingly common in the investigation of arson cases to find that a deliberately set explosion was used to start a fire or that a fire was deliberately accelerated by an explosion.
In investigations, it is often difficult to determine which occurred first-the fire or the explosion.
This difficulty poses a problem for the prosecution when laying a charge in such cases for, at the moment, there are two separate sets of offences in the Code: those relating to causing an explosion (Ss. 79 to 82) and those relating to setting a fire (Ss 433 to 436).
There is always a risk that if the prosecution alleges that the fire was the initial event and the explosion followed and the evidence is to the contrary, the accused will be acquitted.
By providing that the offence is committed by either causing an explosion or setting a fire, this risk is eliminated.

The courts have interpreted the phrase "set fire to" in the present Section 436 somewhat narrowly. Case law has determined that the phrase requires that there be actual combustion to commit arson. Mere scorching, for instance, is not enough even though it may constitute significant damage. Accordingly, to date some individuals who have set fire wilfully have been acquitted owing to the fact that the damage to the property had not reached the degree of combustion required by the case law. To rectify this the definition of the offence has been amended so that any damage to property caused by fire or explosion would constitute arson. This change will ensure that whether or not combustion actually occurs, arsonists will be called upon to account for the damage they cause.
The Law Reform Commission has recommended that arson cover the destruction or damage to all property or real property without distinction. Under the current legislation, setting fire to a vegetable stack is arson while setting fire to someone's car is not. The proposed definition eliminates anomalies such as these by making no distinction among the types of property capable of being damaged.
I also point out the effect of the present Section 436 of the Criminal Code is to deem it to be arson committed by negligence where a loss of life, bodily harm or property damage results from a failure to comply with fire prevention laws by an owner, an occupant of property or person who has control of the property.
The Law Reform Commission recommended that no offence of negligence be retained in the Criminal Code in which the harm caused can only be damage to, or in relation to property. However, many of those consulted argued forcefully that too many owners are lax or negligent in maintaining residential rental units, particularly in disadvantaged areas. Given the destructive nature of fire once it started, it was important to emphasize the fundamental duty of care with regard to fire by clearly warning those who might be inclined to be
February 15, 1990

negligent that they may be charged and convicted before a criminal court.
Even though it is important to retain an offence of negligent arson in the Code, it was important to reformulate it and the presumptions which underpin it so as to minimize any possibility that the offence might be found contrary to the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We have done that in Section 436.
The present provisions on arson contain two presumptions. Under Section 435 the fact that a person holds a fire insurance policy relating to property wilfully set on fire is, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, proof of intent to defraud. Section 436 provides that a person is deemed wilfully to have caused a fire if it is established the fire would not have occurred if the fire prevention by-law had been complied with. We believe that both presumptions are open to challenge under the Charter.
Bill C-53 will amend the present mandatory presumptions to permit permissible inferences. That is, the trier of fact may, not must, infer an intent to defraud from the fact that an owner intentionally caused an explosion or fire to property that was insured. In practice, the proposed permissible inferences should be as effective as the present mandatory presumptions in helping to convict the fraudulent arsonist without, at the same time, infringing on the charter of rights of the accused.
The present Criminal Code does not contain any provisions covering cases where someone is caught with accelerants, gasoline or other similar substances in circumstances indicating that they have these items in order to set a fire. Because mere possession of such materials is itself not a crime, the police must wait until a suspect has taken some substantial step toward setting a fire before making an arrest. By that time it may be too late as the fire may have already begun to bum. To deal with this omission the bill creates a new offence of possession of incendiary materials for the purpose of committing an offence.
In conclusion, a number of representatives of the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police and the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs have already endorsed these amendments, including the North York City Council, which my hon. friend represents.
The fire chief in my constituency in Orillia has been urging action on this issue for many years. I am pleased to advise Chief Shropshire and all fire chiefs and
Government Orders
fire-fighters in Canada that the government has taken action. We want to send a very clear message that arson is a very serious crime. Canadians, especially fire-fighters and innocent bystanders must be given the fullest possible protection from today's sophisticated arsonists.
I ask that the House support these amendments.
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak veiy briefly on this matter. I had no idea that a learned discourse had been prepared on the subject by the minister.

speechtext: I believe the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River does have a short discourse. We will listen to him on debate.

Mr. Speaker, this is not really a legal discourse. I did look forward to addressing the introduction of this bill and its second reading.
What the legislation does signal, of course, is an incredibly large need for reform, not just of this section of the Criminal Code, but many parts of the Criminal Code.
What we have in the old arson sections of the Criminal Code are some very outdated terms. We can see by looking at them just how far the Criminal Code and these provisions have drifted out of date with reality. The old section refers to setting fire to military or public stores. Well, I do not know what public stores really are. In Nova Scotia where I was bom, I think a public store was a liquor store. It refers to timber for fitting out a ship. I have not seen that concept in quite a while. It also refers to stacks of vegetable produce. This is not just a question of cosmetics or the law looking dumb and inexact. It is actually much worse than that. The terms the way they are expressed now provide pitfalls, booby-traps and ambiguities for police and Crown prosecutors right across the country.
For example, with reference to stacks of vegetables, I wonder whether burning a stack of tomatoes would constitute an offence. I suggest that it may well not because tomatoes are not vegetables, they are fruit. The way the old section reads: "Everyone who wilfully sets fire to a stack of vegetable produce, is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment". That is all it says. I question whether or not the simple lighting of a cigarette or several cigarettes is a stack of vegetable produce. These are examples of the difficulties with the old legislation. All of this has implications for cost-effec-

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
tiveness and efficiency in law enforcement and judicial procedures.
We would probably embarrass ourselves if we looked at the costs of mistrials and dismissals as a result of unnecessary loopholes and technical deficiencies in our laws. That is why I am pleased to address these today.
I would add one caution. That is the adoption in the new statutes of the crime of arson by negligence. It is something that the Law Reform Commission has referred to in its previous studies. I am not so sure that we should be creating an offence that is fuzzy or ambiguous in terms of definition and one where society is capable of off-loading its anger or revenge for a destructive fire, a fire that may have caused the loss of life, to someone who may have inadvertently failed to live up to some aspect of a municipal by-law. I think in terms of criminal law for all of our benefit we look for precision and the removal of ambiguity. I hope that the legislative committee will address this issue at the legislative committee stage.
Therefore I would signal our support in principle for adoption of these reforms. I ask the legislative committee to exercise some caution in its meticulous review of Section 436.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the hour I will abandon my lengthy learned discourse on this bill and merely take a couple of minutes to indicate that certainly we support in principle the changes which are being proposed to the Criminal Code in the area of arson.
As the minister indicated, there have been no substantive changes to this section of the Criminal Code since 1892 when the Code was enacted. The statistics are clear. In 1988 approximately 10,500 cases of arson or suspected arson took the lives of 42 people and caused more than $198 million in insurable losses. Of course the actual economic loss is well beyond that. One of the areas I would hope we could look at is the extent to which arson laws in fact are being effectively and vigorously enforced.
This causes particular difficulty to firefighters, many of whom are volunteers and at special risk. I would note that in 1987, for example, some 257 firefighters were
injured on the job. I would like to take this opportunity to pay tribute to firefighters across the country who have done such an outstanding job on behalf of the communities in which they work.
Canadians have lost homes, schools and workplaces to arson. For example, in 1987 in my own province of British Columbia, an elementary school in New Westminster was damaged to the tune of nearly $2 million. There have been losses of that nature across the country.
The minister indicated that there had been extensive consultations on this legislation. One of the groups that does not appear to have been consulted, at least there is no reference to it, is firefighters themselves. Sometimes we forget the people who are on the front lines. I am not talking about the fire chiefs but the International Association of Firefighters. They are the men and women who are in the front lines and I think they deserve to be heard in this area. If they are interested I hope that we could hear from them in the committee. It is not a lengthy process I am talking about but let us give an opportunity to those who are in the front lines. In some cases they have been injured or given their lives.
I would like to make one other comment with respect to this legislation in the context of criminal law reform. This is a rather piecemeal approach to criminal law reform and I would hope that there could be a more comprehensive approach. The Law Reform Commission of Canada has in fact done some important and, indeed, pioneering work in recommending changes to the Code. They have adopted a report on the general part and I know the minister recently indicated in a speech that he is prepared to move forward in this area. Let us hope that at last that movement does come about. The Criminal Code was first adopted in 1892 and it would be appropriate as we near the one hundredth anniversary of the adoption of the first Code to make a commitment on all sides of the House to try to work toward comprehensive reform instead of reform in bits and pieces.
Certainly there are a number of areas that have to be dealt with on an urgent basis. The report of the Marshall inquiry on native justice pointed to a number of areas of concern in terms of criminal law reform and practice. The practice of full disclosure by the Crown is strongly recommended by the Marshall inquiry as a means of
February 15, 1990

helping to avoid the kind the injustice that took place there.
I hope that the Minister of Justice will look very seriously at the necessary amendments in order to achieve full disclosure in the criminal justice process.
Finally, I want to come back to the question of a comprehensive approach to the criminal law and to note in examining the criminal law that the minister should pay careful attention to a study commissioned by the Secretary of State, the minister responsible for the status of women in 1986.
The working group came up with a study entitled "A Feminist Review of Criminal Law". It made a number of excellent recommendations and in the context of comprehensive criminal law reform I hope the government will look at them very seriously.
We have heard from Madam Justice Bertha Wilson on this important question of changes, particularly in the area of criminal law. She said, and I quote, "Some aspects of the criminal law in particular cry out for change since they are based on presuppositions about the nature of women and women's sexuality that in this day and age are a little short of ludicrous".
As well, she pointed out that in some areas of the law a distinctly male perspective is clearly discernible and has resulted in legal principles that are not fundamentally sound and should be revisited as and when the opportunity presents itself. This is a clear invitation to the government to move forward in this important area of criminal law reform and to deal with sexism in the criminal law and in our society.
I hope the minister will move in one particular area, the whole area of sexual assault and the honest belief defence which is clearly susceptible to abuse.
On behalf of my party, I support in principle the legislation we are now dealing with to bring up to date the law on arson in Canada. I want to pay tribute to those groups across the country who have been responsible for bringing this important legislation forward and certainly, as always, to commend the Minister of Justice for bringing forward this legislation in response to the Orillia fire chief as well as fire chiefs and men and women across this country who do such an outstanding job for our communities.
