speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
that Bill C-61, an act to amend the Divorce Act (barriers to religious remarriage), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have another short learned discourse that I want to make. I think it is important to say that I do appreciate the spirit of co-operation this afternoon. One might be tempted to shorten one's speeches-and I have somewhat anyway-but it is important that in the future when somebody says, "Well, why did the government move and why was there not much debate?" I think we could be held accountable for not at least putting on the record why we are going things. So, if I may, I would just like to set out a few thoughts.
The bill before us today is an amendment to the Divorce Act which would provide a court with discretionary powers to preclude a spouse from obtaining relief or proceeding under the Divorce Act where that spouse refuses to remove a barrier to religious remarriage and where the power to remove the barrier to religious remarriage lies solely with that person. Where the court is satisfied that the spouse who refuses to remove the barrier has genuine grounds of a religious or conscientious nature for doing so, it need not exercise its discretion to grant the remedy provided for in this legislation.
Two reasons have prompted the government to present the amendment. First, the Jewish community led by B'nai Brith and the Canadian Jewish Congress, supported by major Jewish organizations, has requested such an amendment to remedy a situation it considers to be unfair. A spouse should not be able to refuse to participate in a Jewish religious divorce-called a Get-in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce. The Get should not be used as a bargaining tool for child custody and access or monetary support.

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
Second, I am concerned about protecting the integrity of the Divorce Act and preventing persons from avoiding the application of the principles contained in the act. For example, a wife may feel compelled to agree to custody arrangements which are not truly in the best interests of a couple's child in order to obtain a Get.
I want to take a few minutes to describe briefly the dilemma certain Jewish persons face because of their religious divorce procedures. In the Jewish religion divorce is accomplished by the delivery of a Get from the husband and its acceptance by the wife in the presence of a Rabbinical Court. According to the Jewish religious traditions, the procedure cannot be changed. Without a Get, a Jewish woman cannot remarry in her own faith. Children of a subsequent civil marriage suffer religious disabilities. While difficult remarriage within the Jewish faith for a man in the same circumstances is not impossible.
In a study conducted by B'nai Brith, husbands were twice as likely as wives to refuse to participate in the Get procedure in order to obtain concessions in a civil divorce. The Jewish community has attempted to solve this problem, but unfortunately they have not been successful.
I just want to say in response to earlier comments by my honourable friend-and I appreciate his comments and compliments-that the government is moving where it can and where it is brought to the government's attention to eliminate sexism and gender bias in the law. I think we have to do it not only in the stated law but in the way the law is applied. It is not perfect.
I say to you as the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada that I think the attention focused on the bias when found in the application of the law is important. That helps us to bring forward changes not only in laws but in people's attitudes, and that is important. While it may be difficult to get the questions in the House, I think it is helpful in that it focuses attention on the issue. I welcome the assistance of all members in dealing with that very important problem.
In preparing for Bill C-611 had two major concerns to resolve. First, the impact on other religious groups and,
second, the consistency of the amendment with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

I did not wish this Bill to affect unintentionally the rules pertaining to religious remarriage of other remarriage of other religious groups in Canada.
Thus, I consulted the leaders of fifty religious groups in Canada, described the elements of the proposed amendment and solicited their comments on the impact of the bill on their respective religious practices. Of the fifty religious groups consulted, nineteen responded with substantive comments.
Mr. Speaker, this consultation process was extremely valuable. It provided us with the opportunity to carefully consider and discuss a number of the important issues this proposed legislation raised.
You will be interested to know the Roman Catholic, Presbyterian and Anglican churches agree with the purpose of this legislation.

I believe that Bill C-61 is consistent with the guarantees of freedom of religion and equality contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms for three reasons.
First, pursuant to the case law developed by the Supreme Court of Canada, subsection 2(a) of the Charter respecting freedom of religion is not necessarily infringed by a law that has a religious dimension, if that law does not interfere with the freedom of individuals affected by it to act on conscientious or religious grounds. The proposed amendment will apply only to the situation where a Get is being refused in order to give the party to a divorce an additional bargaining tool for the civil divorce, not because the person is refusing on religious or conscientious grounds. In Judaism there are no religious grounds to refuse the Get.
Second, Section 15 guaranteeing equality of persons does not require that all members of society be treated identically if their needs require otherwise. In the present circumstances, although the Jewish community is the group primarily affected by the proposed amendment, this is because of the particular problems that it has experienced. Specifically, it has no recourse to a
February 15, 1990

religious tribunal as do all other religious groups canvassed that have religious divorce proceedings.
Third, even if a prima facie case were made for a breach of the freedom of religion, I believe the proposal is still defensible under Section 1 of the Charter as a reasonable limit. Such a limit would ensure, for example, that custody decisions were made according to the child's best interest as required under the Divorce Act and not as a result of concessions in exchange for a Get. While impact on other religions and Charter implications were major concerns, I would also like to address two other considerations.
[Translation}
First, I have encountered on occasion the view that this amendment may set a precedent regarding other difficulties of other religions. No one, however, has actually been able to point to any situation similar to that of the Get.
It is the case that in some religions, the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox and Islam, annulment or divorce may proceed more easily and faster if the couple agree.
However, in all these cases, the authority to grant the annulment or divorce rests with the religious tribunal, not the couple.
An un-co-operative spouse may delay a decision, but ultimately he or she cannot prevent the religious tribunal from rendering its decision.
In these religions, the spouse initiating the action can ask the religious authorities to deal with this problem.
The Jewish spouse does not have that recourse. [English]
Second, the current provisions of the Divorce Act were examined thoroughly to determine if they provided a remedy. The conclusion was that they did not.
I say in conclusion that Bill C-61 can accomplish three objectives. First, it answers the request from the Jewish community for legislative support to rectify a situation it considers unfair. Jewish persons who wish to remarry within their faith will have a greater opportunity to do so.
Second, it protects the integrity of the government's own legislation, the Divorce Act, by ensuring that con-
Govemment Orders
cessions are not made on support, custody or access in exchange for religious divorce.
Third, the amendment does not appear to have an impact upon other religious groups. National Jewish groups have already indicated their support for the proposed amendments. The B'nai Brith made this comment in a communique on the day we introduced it: "Canadians should be proud that their government is prepared to make its multiculturalism policy a living reality by undertaking actions as this." The Canadian Jewish Congress commended the federal government for introducing the legislation.
I would ask all members of the House to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I also welcome this important amendment to the Divorce Act and I want to commend the minister for bringing it forward.
It is a bill that means a great deal in the Jewish community of which I am a member. I have been part of the process over the years of looking for solutions to a situation in Halachic law, which is the Jewish traditional law that puts women at a very considerable disadvantage when civil divorces are granted. I am happy that the minister has brought it forward today. I was very glad that we were able to sit through the lunch hour in order to get this bill through, together with some other justice bills.
I must confess to be dazzled at the display of learning about Jewish traditional law that the minister has just shown, and I am look forward to the bill going to committee. I do not think this is a controversial bill. I know it is a bill with all-partisan support.
I want also to express some appreciation for the consideration which this bill was given and for the positive support which it received from the other religious and ethnic communities of our country that were approached for comment about this bill. None of them, as we anticipated, would find that this bill made life more difficult for them, nor does this bill entrench in any way on civil or religious freedom in Canada. However, it would not have been difficult to imagine obstacles being put forward just for the sake of making life difficult. I think it is a tribute to the good state of relations among

February 15, 1990
Government Orders
the various groups which proudly make up the fabric of Canada that no such obstacles emerged.
We are faced with a situation in which we can look forward to an accommodation. In a country which is pluralistic, bilingual and multicultural, a measure like this, the result that it has achieved and the support that it has received so far is a good sign of the accommodations that Canadians are prepared to make to reinforce and strengthen the national fabric.
Many people, as do I, visualize lots of possible and potential tensions among the various groups within Canada. Multiculturalism and pluralism is a new kind of national experience. Canada is not a country that has the benefit of a monolithic, racial, religious, cultural group which views the nation as an expression of its identity. Most countries are like that. By contrast, our country is a country whose most basic identity comes from the accommodation of minority groups, from the tolerance of differences and from respect for differences, something which is even better than mere tolerance.
We are making our country work when we accommodate legislation like this. We are helping to set an example for others in the country. I want to express the pleasure that I feel at seeing this important step, demonstrating again the openness of this great country of ours.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the Elouse was able to agree unanimously to extend the hours to deal with this important legislation. I want to pay tribute to all members of the House who co-operated in this regard, particularly the member for York Centre who was instrumental in achieving this.
This legislation is legislation for which on behalf of the New Democratic Party I have called for some time. I welcome the government's decision to move forward on it at this moment.
I recall, as I am sure my colleague from York Centre will recall, and indeed I believe my colleague from Niagara Falls was in the House and the committee at that time as well, that during debates on the Divorce Act
in 1985 and 1986 there were discussions on this subject. At that point I made it clear that certainly in principle we supported this amendment.
On January 23, 1986, the then Minister of Justice, the member for St. John's West, said this: "I have instructed my officials to establish an expeditious process of consultation with representatives of all the various interests in order to resolve these outstanding issues".
Four years later that expeditious process has resulted in this legislation. I think it is not a minute too soon. I am going to give a couple of examples of the practical effect of the absence of this legislation on women in this country who have suffered as a result.
I want to pay tribute to the many groups and individuals across Canada who have played such an important role in this historic legislation. Those groups include B'nai Brith, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Coalition of Jewish Women for the Get, and a broad range of others.
I want to single out in particular the contribution of a lawyer, John Syrtash, who has done an extraordinary job on behalf of the coalition that has been seeking changes in this law and, in many ways, who was instrumental as well in achieving changes to provincial legislation in the province of Ontario in 1986.
Following the decision of the Minister of Justice to look into this matter, B'nai Brith Canada conducted a comprehensive study on the use of the Get as a bargaining tool in Jewish divorce proceedings. That study pointed out, and it has already been noted, that Jews who are loyal to the teachings and practices of their faith are not free to enter into a second marriage unless the prior marriage has been terminated either by the death of the spouse or by the execution of the divorce procedure recognized by Halacha, which is Jewish law.
This study documented that in some 311 cases the refusal to issue a Get resulted in very substantial pain and difficulty to one of the spouses. The vast majority of those spouses affected-in some 202 of the cases-are in fact women who were affected by their husband's refusal to grant the Get. There were certainly as well some instances of women who refused to consent to the Get. The reality is that it is primarily Jewish women who have been hurt by this requirement.
February 15, 1990

I want to spend just a couple of minutes in terms of the background of this. I think it is important that we recognize what has led to this legislation because I believe it is the first in the world at the national level.
One of the commentators on the subject, a woman named Norma Joseph who participated in a forum in Montreal in October, 1988, gave some of the background. She pointed out that mutual consent constitutes sufficient grounds for a Jewish divorce; and that if both parties agree they appear before three rabbis who constitute a Beth Din, or Jewish court.
The fact is that the process in the Beth Din was supposed to set both parties free, but in fact in some cases there are partners, particularly women, who are unfree, who are chained, Agunot, Jews who are divorced who cannot obtain the Get. The definition of Agunah or Agun is someone who is tied, chained or anchored to an absent spouse.
I mentioned that this can theoretically affect both men and women, but because of the structure of Jewish law the victim in fact is most frequently a woman. Since a man must give the Get she is left dependent upon his action.
Rabbinical law was amended to include her acceptance of the document but in fact the Beth Din or the rabbinical court can act in a way to release the man without her co-operation but never the other way around.
I mentioned that I wanted to give some practical examples. I think it is important to do that so Canadians who are not familiar with the implications of the Get, as certainly I was not before this was brought to my attention, will realize the significance of what Parliament is doing. I want to thank Norma Joseph for the work she has done in bringing this matter to the attention of parliamentarians and the public.
These are some examples. The first involves an elderly woman, divorced 35 years in Quebec. Finally, she falls in love. She finds someone to take care of her, to share with her, to live with her but she has no Get. She raised her children alone. She did not ask for money and she did not in any way bother her first husband. All she wanted was to be free, to end her days in companionship and love. But without the Get she cannot remarry.
Government Orders
Another example involves a young woman who had no children but who had a business. Her ex-husband said: "Okay, I will give you the Get but you renounce your share of our business".
There is the case of a professional, a social worker, who would not give the Get out of revenge because, he said, his wife did not deserve it.
One of the most frequent abuses of this Get procedure is the husband who says: "Sure, I will give you the Get. You just give me $35,000, or $50,000, or $75,000". That is extortion, and that is exactly what this legislation is attempting to deal with.
What about the young woman whose husband has disappeared? She cannot obtain the Get.
One other example involves a woman who married an immigrant. She was to sponsor him in Canada. Things went sour. She instituted divorce proceedings and he said: "No. I will refuse to co-operate with the Get". The social worker who was called in to help advised that she be co-operative and not vindictive: "Sign his immigrant papers. Show him how nice you can be". It was bad advice. He is now a landed immigrant and she is an Agunah, chained, denied that divorce.
It is precisely because of that abuse, the potential for extortion, that this legislation is so important.
I recognize the argument that has been made that we have to very jealously guard the division between church and state. I strongly support that.
As well, I recognize there are some who suggest, including some within the Jewish community, that this is not a matter that should be dealt with by means of legislation. They believe that it is something that should be worked out within the Jewish community; that it should be worked out by the rabbis. Some people say: "If Parliament acts, then that removes the pressure on rabbinic leaders to amend religious law to give women equal status in Jewish divorce proceedings".
Certainly, I fully agree that Jewish lay and rabbinic leaders should be taking steps to reconcile the fact that Jewish women outside Canada will remain disenfranchised with their support for this legislation. I hope that that will happen.

February 15, 1990
In fact, one of the suggestions that has been made is that an international panel of rabbinic authorities confront this religious law which is so clearly in need of change. That would help to ensure that Jewish women everywhere, not just in Canada, would be treated with dignity and respect as they are entitled to be.
The Halachic solution, the solution within the Jewish community, is an important solution. I note that steps have been taken in that regard already.
I want to pay tribute to the Rabbinic Council of Canada, Quebec Region which, with the approval of the Vaad Harabonim, have instituted a pre-nuptical agreement. Hopefully, these will not be necessary any more. But they did show leadership and I want to pay tribute to them for doing that. I hope now the community will move to deal with this injustice, hopefully on an international scale.
In conclusion, we in the New Democratic Party support this important legislation. We have urged its adoption for some time. I know my colleague for Vancouver East in her capacity as the spokesperson on the status of women has dealt with this important question. My colleague for Thunder Bay-Atikokan, who in particular wanted to be here for this debate but because of the scheduling was unable to, wanted to speak to his support for this bill. Indeed, he, along with the hon. member for Mission-Coquitlam and my other colleagues have worked hard with me to bring this legislation about.
This legislation is legislation that is overdue. It will help to ease the pain and the anguish of people who have been denied the Get. We welcome it. We pay tribute to those organizations and individuals who are responsible for bringing it about, for making us the first country in the world to adopt this legislation.
I hope that the legislative committee will move expeditiously to ensure that this becomes law so that no other woman or man will be denied the Get.

Mr. Speaker, the report released by the Canadian Institute of Child Health is a voice for Canadian children. It is a documented cry for help and the government of Canada must react, and react immediately.
The health care of our nation's children is being neglected. The situation is not going to change until some very progressive moves are made in the areas of social and economic development and, just as importantly, social and economic equality.
We have the best hospitals in the world, the best doctors in the world, but until social and economic concerns are addressed, the health of Canadian children will remain as shameful as reported by the Canadian Institute of Child Health.
We need some answers to some very important questions. For example, why do we have so little data on mental health? Why are so many young people committing suicide? We have to look at why our young people are feeling so lost, what is happening out there that is destroying all of their dreams and their aspirations.
In 1986, the death rate for poor children was 56 per cent higher than those of higher income children. The mortality rates for our native infants are twice the rate of the total population. Health care does not just mean medicine. Health care is integrally linked to social and economic conditions.
Children are our guarantee of a future. We are relying on them for tomorrow, just as much as they are relying on us today.
February 15, 1990

Mr. Speaker, today is a proud one for Canada as we celebrate the twenty-fifth anniversary of our flag.
However, last Tuesday our country's image was disrespected by a motion placed before this House about racism and bigotry, the very wording of which was mean-spirited, intolerant and insensitive.
It is constructive to make objective criticisms and to propose effective new initiatives to combat racism and bigotry in Canada. It is quite a different matter, and it is destructive, to use these sensitive and critical issues, as that motion did, in sweeping generalities about the character of our country for purposes of political gain.
The political unity and social integrity of our nation are goals which transcend partisan considerations, and every member of this House should feel a sense of partnership in our common effort to make this country whole.
Certainly, we must all do better and we must all do more. But let us recognize that much has already been done to build a unique and enriched society in Canada of which all Canadians should be justly proud.
Let us not in this House be found to be found to be the cause of racial and linguistic division in Canada. Rather, let us always strive to represent together the true course toward complete Canadian unity.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was most disturbed to learn yesterday that Harrod's of London, after 15 years of selling Canadian fur products, is closing its fur salon because of declining demand.
This comes on the heels of the Hudson Bay Company moving its European auction house to Helsinki, ending a century old presence in Britain.
These events should concern all Canadians. The Canadian fur trade contributes over $1 billion to the national economy and well over $300 million is brought into the country through fur exports.
As staunch supporters of the Canadian fur industry, this government recognizes that our fur exports to the United States and to Europe are significant to the health
of the industry. The announcement of Harrod's is not good news for Canadian fur exporters.
I call upon my colleagues in the House to work closely with the fur industry, the fur association, and hundreds of northern communities where fur is the economic lifeline to overcome this temporary situation in the market-place. Our continued support for Canadian quality fur products will ensure that there will be no further unwelcome news from Europe and abroad.

Mr. Speaker, once again Canadians are being subjected to Conservative warnings to "prepare for a tough budget" consisting, no doubt, of even deeper cuts to once sacred social programs and more unfair tax hikes.
This year something new has been added to a tired script: an obsession with secrecy. The Minister of Finance says he is too busy and he is refusing to hold his usual pre-budget consultations and delaying the distribution of the budget until after it has been tabled. This flies in the face of the opinion of his Prime Minister regarding budgetary reform. In his book, Where I Stand, it states: "In an age when we know that government works best when it builds a consensus of public understanding"-I repeat, Mr. Speaker, a consensus of public understanding-"the budget is dropped out of nowhere one night with virtually no effort having been made to achieve agreement or even understanding of its principal goals." The Prime Minister continues: "No process in the world will prevent bad decision-making, but the present budget-making process itself contributes to bad decisionmaking and therefore to bad government."
New Democrats could not agree more.

Mr. Speaker, the constitutional debate and language issues are now attracting a lot of national attention. I would like to draw heavily on an editorial in this morning's La Presse by Pierre Gravel to urge Canadians to be calm and moderate in their statements and discussions. Relations between anglophones and francophones are becoming increasingly vexed these days. The slightest initiative looks like a

February 15, 1990
declaration of war, bad faith sets in and barriers go up between different groups in our population.
Many in our country are on edge at a time when it is more important than ever for cool heads, the editorialist reminds us. I therefore suggest that Canadians try to deepen the language debate and make an effort to better understand the whole philosophy behind the Meech Lake Agreement. We will really understand each other, Mr. Speaker, when we each put good will in our contacts, dealings and discussions. It is certainly possible to discuss and express opinions with as much dignity, respect and equanimity as possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were very sorry to learn this morning of the death of Georges Forest, a great Canadian and great Manitoban. As you may recall, Georges Forest became known for his tireless efforts to defend the rights of linguistic minorities in Manitoba.
In a spirit of openness and tolerance, Georges Forest relentlessly pursued his cause to the Supreme Court of Canada, which ruled in his favour. By this historic act, he corrected 100 years of injustice to Manitoba's francophones. Mr. Forest was not a vengeful man. Mr. Forest was a great Canadian who believed in the principle of linguistic duality and respect for minority rights.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to him today and I ask this Flouse to join me in extending our sincerest condolences to his family. This great patriot has made his mark.
* *

Mr. Speaker, we all know that across Canada there are very strong feelings and loud opinions being expressed about the proposed GST. I am concerned that there are some irresponsible people
advising others to protest the tax by not submitting their applications for the GST credit included with the 1989 income tax form.
Next year, a family with two children and $20,000 net income who would have received a $10 FST credit in 1988, will be eligible for a GST credit of $580. A senior with a net income of $20,000 is eligible for a GST credit of $290 in 1991.
This credit is designed to assist low-income earners. Most of the irresponsible advice to boycott the rebate form is coming from those who, by virtue of high income, would not be eligible for it. I would urge those who are eligible, whether they support the tax or not, to complete the form and take advantage of the credit.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Minister of National Health and Welfare responded to my question about the muzzling of government advisoiy groups with the threat of budget cuts, by saying that if I had bothered to listen to the radio, his deputy minister had made it abundantly dear that no such suggestion was made.
I suggest that the Minister might want to read today's Citizen where his deputy minister is directly quoted as saying:
It's like having the heads of one of my departments, or indeed me,
saying this is a crummy piece of government policy-
I remind the minister that the National Council on Welfare is a citizens' advisoiy body and has included, among its members, not only welfare recipients, public housing tenants and low-income citizens, but lawyers, professionals and social workers. The executive director is accountable to the council, not to the minister, and the council has a mandate to advise this government on poverty and social issues.
Ministers muzzling advisory bodies who tell it like it is does not make crummy policy good, it makes crummy policy crummy law.
February 15, 1990

speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Science and Technology)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Science and Technology)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fire now raging in a stockpile of discarded tires in Hagersville, Ontario, has revived fears about the hazard posed by these sites.
I think it is absolutely essential and urgent that measures to get rid of these stockpiles be taken as soon as possible. That is why we would like to bring the following to the attention of the House. Dr. Christian Roy, an engineer at Laval University, has been working for several years, with the support of the federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, on a technique called pyrolysis under vacuum, which can be used to recycle old tires.
The tires are burned in lead tanks equipped with a vacuum pump to draw off the gaseous products, thus preventing contaminants from entering the atmosphere.
With this process, practically the whole tire can be recycled, 65 per cent as oil and 25 per cent in the form of carbon black, which products can then be sold back to the industry.
Every year 25 million tires are produced in Canada. Clearly, we must stop stockpiling these discarded tires and start using other methods to get rid of them.
Personally, I think the vacuum pyrolysis technique developed by Dr. Roy might be the answer. That is why the government should make this new technology one of its priorities.

Mr. Speaker, after having incurred the wrath of nearly every Canadian taxpayer through his proposed goods and services tax, the Minister of Finance has sunk to a new low.
Indeed, 20 years after the proclamation of the Official Languages Act, that minister has the temerity to insult
my constituents by providing them with brochures in only one of the official languages, extolling the dubious virtues of his infamous GST.
Need I remind the minister that the riding of Restigouche-Chaleur is composed of a bilingual population and that New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province in Canada.
My constituents expect to receive bilingual services and the government has the obligation to provide them.

The people of St-Quentin are upset because of this brochure, and rightly so. They asked me why, in 1990, Francophones still have to ask to get information in French, even when it comes from the seat of government of a bilingual country. They also wonder whether the GST is something only Anglophones have to understand.
At a time when there is a real language crisis in this country, the minister should have avoided aggravating the problem and made sure that information on the GST was distributed in both official languages.

subtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said that this century would be Canada's. We are now in the century's last decade, and I think can say that our country did in fact, reach maturity during the second half of the twentieth century.
Our flag, whose 25th anniversary it is today, testifies better than any other emblem to the maturity of our country. Drawing from the traditions of people from all over the world, as well as from our own experience, we have become mature as a nation worthy of the name.
Our flag is a precious part of our heritage. Its symbolism goes deep into our collective soul and has hepled to promote our identity as a people.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to quote what was said by the hon. Maurice Bourget, Speaker of the Senate, on February 15, 1965: "The flag is a symbol of the unity of our country, since there can be no doubt that it represents all citizens of Canada, regardless of race, language, creed or opinion".

February 15, 1990
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, today marks the twenty-fifth anniversary of the Canadian flag.
Hear, hear!

It was 25 years ago that our distinctive red maple leaf flag was raised over this building for the very first time.
John Matheson, a former MP from Leeds was credited at that time by Prime Minister Pearson as "the one man who had more to do with having a Canadian flag than any other.''
Today, we salute John Matheson and all proud Canadians as we celebrate the silver anniversary of Canada's very own distinctive red maple leaf flag.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand an incredible article which begins with the headline: "Edmonston does flip-flop: Now he's opposing Meech". I want to quote from the article which states:
During the Party's leadership convention in December, Edmonston reacted bitterly to a compromise resolution seeking changes to Meech.
Delegates accepted it in an effort to reconcile supporters of the accord and members who wanted major changes.
"You can't have your cake and eat it, too. I'm not saying that to be menacing or to blackmail you," Edmonston warned the convention, saying the resolution was a vote against Meech and Quebec.
The article further states:
During the by-election campaign Edmondston simply pretended the NDP's position didn't exist, campaigning on a platform of total acceptance of the deal without amendments.
The article further states:
He turned his back yesterday on the no-compromise, pro-Meech position that helped him win a stunning landslide victory in Monday's Chambly, Quebec, by-election.
He says: "I support the party (position) entirely". Cynical? You bet. I will bet you the poor people of Chambly are scratching their heads today.

Mr. Speaker, a few years ago I fought to save The Friendly Giant from budget cuts at the CBC. Well, last week was like a replay of a bad dream. It started with the cancellation of Switchback, a wonderful regionally produced youth services on CBC television. It ended with the news that Conservative policies, including the GST and cuts to postal subsidies may kill off Owl and Chickadee magazines, this at a time when we want to encourage reading and environmental awareness among our children.
This governing is slamming the Polka Dot Door on children's entertainment. What is next? Contracting out Casey and Finnegan's jobs to a pair of non-union Smurfs?
The issue is more than just entertainment. The shaping of young minds will happen whether we act or not. All we can influence is who does the shaping and how.
It can be done by Nintendo, Rambo and G.I. Joe, or it can be done with a view to the future, with intelligent media programming and rich, valuable reading. The choice is ours.

Mr. Speaker, the pigeons have come home to roost. The Bank of Canada interest rate is at 13.32 per cent, an all-time high since the recession of the early 1980s.
My question is for the Minister of Finance. Will he acknowledge that his prediction in the budget last year that we would be enjoying rates around 10 per cent at this stage of the game, was a total and unmitigated failure? The Minister of Finance has to tell Canadians and the money markets, investors and business people what is the policy of this government on interest rates in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have made it abundantly clear what the policy is, not just yesterday, not just the day before, but for many months now.
With the instability and the volatility in the markets today, our first objective is to gain stability in those markets, and second, on an ongoing basis, to reduce the level of inflation so that we can get interest rates down.
I acknowledge what my hon. friend has said. Interest rates have stayed up longer than we had anticipated last April. The reason is that inflationary pressures have been stronger and the economy has been stronger than we had anticipated in April. I might add that they are stronger than many other economic forecasters had anticipated last April.
Once we get inflation under control, we will be able to see some easing in interest rates. But until we see some real progress in getting inflation under control, we will not be able to see any meaningful reduction in interest rates.

Mr. Speaker, is the minister prepared to at least admit that the contradictory statements made by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, Conservative backbenchers and the Governor of the Bank of Canada contribute to the uncertainty among Canadians and investors here and abroad? My question for the Finance Minister is: Do Canadians not deserve a coherent, comprehensible policy from this government after five years in power? Is he prepared to articulate such a coherent policy in order to reassure investors that the Government of Canada knows where it is going?

Mr. Speaker, above all, what investors, whether they are Canadian or foreign, have received over the last five years is a coherent economic policy. This coherent policy was first set out in November 8, 1984 in the Agenda for Economic Renewal where we stated clearly the two prongs of our economic strategy: first, to get our financial house in order, and second, to deal with some of the structural problems that were causing inefficiencies in our economy. We have followed what we set out to do in
Oral Questions
November 8, 1984 in a very careful, consistent and coherent way.
The results have been very clear. In Canada, we have had economic growth only a small margin behind that of Japan. We have had the best job-creation record of any of the major industrialized countries through that period, and precisely because Canadians and foreign investors could understand exactly where we were going as a country because it was all set out in that document of November 8, 1984.

Mr. Speaker, interest rates are going up, the dollar is going down, the government is going where even angels fear to tred.
The question that the finance minister has to address and that I put to him today is that just last Friday the Prime Minister was saying after the budget is introduced next week, the interest rates are going to go down. Interest rates today are up to an unparalleled height since the Minister of Finance came into office. The rates are going up this week. Are they going to go down next week? Does the minister have a policy, and how is he going to explain to Canadians that he is saying one thing and the Prime Minister is saying another?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is absolutely wrong and he knows that he is wrong. If he had taken the time to read the transcript of what the Prime Minister said, he would have seen that it was exactly what I have been saying over the past number of weeks. I say to him, read it before trying to sow this uncertainty in the minds of Canadians.
I have made it very clear that if people want to see lower interest rates then we have to see lower inflation. Until we get lower inflation, we are not going to see lower interest rates. It is as simple as that. That is what we have been striving to do with our interest rate policy, and that is what we have been striving to do in our fiscal policy.
Every time this government has tried to do something to get our expenses down, to get the deficit down and to get the debt problem under control, every time we have put something on the table that party, as well as the New Democratic Party, have fought tooth and nail to try to stop us doing these things. These are the things that we are committed to do. We are going to do them because

February 15, 1990
Oral Questions
they are right for the country and they are going to result in a much healthier economic environment.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, this government's high interest rate policies are hammering Canadian exporters. It means that they have to pay more to modernize and be competitive. It means that the artificially high dollar created by this government is a far greater burden on our Canadian exporters than the U.S. interest rates were that this free trade deal purported to eliminate.
Let us look at the results of this government's coherent economic policies for the last five and one-half years. When this government took office the government's current account surplus with other nations was $3.1 billion. Today, we have a record deficit of $20 billion. When will this government realize that its high interest rates have straitjacketed Canadian producers, that they are costing us exports and that they are costing us jobs?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member fails to point out that one of the reasons for that current account deficit is that companies have been investing in the future because they have confidence in the future. When they invest in the future they buy that machinery and equipment in large part from other countries. That is one of the major reasons why our current account deficit has increased over the past few years because we have had record investment in Canada reflecting the confidence that people have had in the future of this country and in the policies that this government has been following.
I understand some of the concerns that the hon. member has mentioned about high interest rates and about the level of the Canadian dollar. I understand the impact that this can have on Canadians, but I ask him to consider the alternative.
If we let interest rates go down in an unnatural way and fire that over-heating inflation, what is going to happen to the inflation rate in this country? What is going to happen to the permanent, competitive position of the very people for whom he purports to be speaking? It will be damaged on a permanent basis and we will have interest rates that are permanently too high. That is what
we had in the seventies and early eighties. That brought the most serious recession this country has seen since the thirties and that is what we are going to avoid.

Mr. Speaker, our producers cannot compete when their interest rates are over 14 per cent and the Japanese producers are paying less than 5 per cent.
My second question involves our second deficit, the budget deficit. By increasing interest rates in Canada last year, in one year alone the government added $6 billion to our national debt. With our twin deficits, a record current account deficit now, and our record national debt, these are a direct result of this government's economic mismanagement.
When will the government stop sacrificing Canada's economic future on the altar of high interest rates?

Mr. Speaker, I do not know who the hon. member is trying to impress, but I can tell him one group of people he would not impress is international investors. If he were standing in my position making those same comments, he can be sure that the dollar would be falling through the floor and we would see interest rates go up further. That is what we are trying to avoid.
The hon. member talks about deficits. Let me remind him that the operating account of the government, that is revenues less program spending, was in a deficit position when we were elected in 1984. In other words, we were spending $16 billion more on government programs than we were taking in. That has now reversed itself. It is a $9 billion surplus. We are making good progress and one of the reasons why we have made good progress is we have controlled government spending.
I say to the hon. member, has he or has his party given us one place where we could reduce program spending in the last five and a half years? I do not remember one.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a question for the Minister of Finance.
The Bank of Canada has just raised the interest rate to 13.32 per cent, an increase of 53 basis points, Mr. Speaker. That is incredible!
February 15, 1990

I think that we are almost on the verge of a monetary crisis in this country. For that reason, I would like to ask the Finance Minister this question. Yesterday, he told the House that there would be cuts in social programs such as education, health and transfers to the provinces because of the Canadian deficit which is too high.
Mr. Speaker, given the rise in interest rates this afternoon, I would like to know whether the Minister of Finance can now explain exactly how much will be cut from social programs next week in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is a very substantial distortion by the hon. member of what I said in the House yesterday, but I guess that is not surprising. That usually comes from that hon. member almost every time he asks a question.
He has asked me to say to him what would be in the budget next week. He knows that it is not possible for me to comment. What I would say to him is if he has some ideas on how we can cut government program spending in a sensible, sensitive way, as we know we must in this country, then I would welcome his suggestions. But again, I have not received any suggestions from him or his colleagues on that score for the last five and half years.

Mr. Speaker, we have told the Minister of Finance a number of times he can cut out some of the grants to his corporate friends in this country and save billions of dollars.
I do not know if the Minister of Finance realizes that we are almost in a very serious economic crisis in this country. The bank rate has jumped .5 per cent today, by 53 basis points.
The Prime Minister predicted just last week that the bank rate in this country would be down before Christmas. I want the Minister of Finance to tell the House today how he is going to bring down the bank rate in this country without cutting back on social programs, programs for the poor, or health, education and transfers to seven provinces of this country. How is he going to do that without hurting the ordinary people?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member suggests that we should cut subsidies to business, grants to business. I would like to draw to his attention that those grants, those subsidies involve subsidies for agriculture, social housing, regional development, research and development. That amounts to the vast majority of what he would classify in the government expenditures as subsidies to business.
Which ones of those subsidies is he saying we should cut, because they are not easy to cut? Each one of those is important. They are important objectives of the Government of Canada, and I believe of his party as well. So come clean, let us know which one of those subsidies you would like to see us cut.

The Minister must recognize that his high interest rate policy has created the problem in agriculture. If you compare the government's intervention to hold up the value of the Canadian dollar through the Bank of Canada's high interest rates with that same government's instructions to farmers via FCC, to "Face up to the market realities in assessing their viability", I have to ask the Minister of Finance to explain why he has not faced up to the same market realities he espouses, permitting the Canadian dollar to fall, thus reflecting its true unmanipulated market value and allowing farm prices to rise?

Mr. Speaker, these are all very worthy objectives that the hon. member would like to see happen. We would all like to see lower interest rates. But we on this side know that you cannot just snap your fingers and make it happen.
The only way it can happen is if the fundamentals of the economy will support a lower level of interest rates. The extent of inflationary pressures that are in the economy today simply do not support that.
The hon. member is telling us to bring down interest rates in an unnatural way, stoke up the fires of inflation, go right back to what we had in 1982. If he is saying that his farm friends in Saskatchewan are saying they want to have the 20 per cent plus interest rates that we had in 1981-82,1 think he is wrong. We do not support that. We are doing everything we can to get inflation down so we can get interest rates down in a permanent way, not the "pie in the sky way" that the hon. member would like to see us have.

February 15, 1990
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. On page 2 of its pre-budgetary brief to the Minister of Finance concerning the GST, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business states that the small grocery stores will be especially affected and will experience tremendous enforcement problems which will compell a great many of them to close.
How could the minister claim in his Information for Convenience Stores bulletin that the necessary paperwork will be kept at a minimum, when in his brief John Bullock says it will not? Who knows small business better, John Bullock or the Minister of Finance?
[English)

Mr. Speaker, I think that the hon. member is distorting what was said in that brochure. We have said right from the start that we are happy and are working with members of the small business community to address this concern. We understand the concern. We understand that they do not want to have any unnecessary complexities as a result of the GST.
We have said that there are two ways of simplified accounting, and that there are more ways of developing simplified accounting systems. We are quite happy to consider those ways to help those grocers and the retailers he talks about.
Over the course of this year we will have representatives from National Revenue, as my colleague, the Minister of National of Revenue has said, to meet on a one-on-one basis to help the members of the small business community understand what is required of them and how the GST will affect their purchasing and pricing so that they can have an easy transition into the new system and avoid the problems that we know they are concerned about. That is why we are going to this extent to solve those problems.

Mr. Speaker, the minister talks about a simplified accounting system. How can he simplify an accounting system when, if you sell yogurt or pudding on an individual basis, it is taxable? If you sell the same products in a group or package, where there is more than one, then it is taxable. What kind of an accounting system does he believe a small comerstore will need to meet his proposal? Why will the minister not withdraw the measure and make it simple for everybody?

Mr. Speaker, I acknowledge that that is one of the difficult borderlines between what is basic groceries and what is taxable foods.
I do not think the hon. member would like to see us tax basic groceries, so we have to draw the borderline somewhere.
One of the objectives of the simplified accounting system is to allow the retailer to account for those without having to calculate each item on an individual basis as they go by his cash register. The purpose of the simplified accounting is so that he can step back and look at the over-all books of accounts and, in that way, have a much simpler way of calculating what tax is owing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. Dozens of protesters gathered in sub-zero temperatures in Brandon, Manitoba, yesterday to tell the Prime Minister exactly how they feel about the GST. Apparently the Prime Minister was not in any mood to listen. He and his entourage just sped by.
One protester was heard to say, "It is a crime that we elect these people, then we have to have demos like this to get our message across". The message is quite clear. They do not want the GST and they are fed up paying Tory taxes.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance today whether he can assure Canadians that come next week's Budget there will be no new taxes and no increases in existing taxes?

Mr. Speaker, we acknowledge that there are people in the country who are opposed to the GST. We also know that
February 15, 1990

at the Prime Minister's dinner, there were 450 people who listened attentively to what he had to say about the GST.
As a result of the Prime Minister's speech, they realized the benefits of the GST and how it will improve our ability to export, and how it will put Canadian producers on a level playing field with importers. Importers now have one-third less tax to pay than the Canadian producers. Also, they learned how it will help the farm community by giving them a full rebate on tax on all farm inputs. These are the benefits that are going to be gained by various sectors in the economy.
I will always come back to the same point. I have listened carefully to what hon. members in the Liberal Party have to say about the GST. They are full of complaints, but they do not have one alternative. They do not know where to go. If we said today, "No GST", they would have their mouths absolutely wide open with nothing to say because they do not know what the alternatives are.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the minister says there were 450 at the meeting. Yes, but they were all carefully selected.
The Minister of Finance will be debating the GST with our finance critic in Edmonton on March 5, but the tickets are by invitation only and they are going to cost $100. That, to me, is an outrage.
I want to ask the finance minister whether he would consider attending another meeting in Edmonton the same day, where the admission price might be free so that ordinary Canadians do not feel locked out of the process and where they can put their questions and concerns directly to the finance minister? It seems to me that if the finance minister wants to elaborate on the GST this will be an excellent opportunity for him.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the thoughtfulness of the hon. member. He should know that that particular debate is going to be on national television. Surely that is going to give Canadians from coast to coast an opportunity to listen and see the nature of the debate.
Another selected audience.

Hon. members would like me to respond to questions. I have been on many,
Oral Questions
many open line shows, coast to coast. The week before I am going to be on three open line shows in British Columbia. I believe I am going to be on an open line show in Edmonton the same day as the debate on March 5. I am happy to do this on an ongoing basis because I have confidence that the GST is right for this country. It is going to put our country in a more competitive position. It will also avoid $2 billion worth of tax avoidance.
Now if the Liberal Party of Canada is in favour of $2 billion of tax avoidance, it is great to hear it because these are the things that we have been trying to stamp out for the last five and a half years, and we have been making good strides in doing so.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. I met today with workers from Varta Batteries Investment Canada. Some 175 workers face job losses in Winnipeg because of the U.S. takeover and shutdown at Varta.
Investment Canada admitted that its review had not taken account of the spin-off job losses at Canada Medals and Reliance Plastics. I want to ask the Minister how he can possibly justify a decision which did not take into account these important points in terms of economic impact.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this particular company was losing substantial amounts of money and it was simply a case of their going bankrupt if we did not allow someone to purchase them. I suppose we could have nationalized them, but if that is what he is advocating we will take a look at it. The alternatives were very limited because of the financial situation of that company.

Mr. Speaker, in fact, the Manitoba government claimed that some workers from Winnipeg would be transferred as part of this takeover to the remaining St. Thomas plant which was going to be kept in operation. But this week we learned that 35 workers at the St. Thomas plant have also been given layoffs.
Why has the minister approved a takeover and a shutdown which has lost us one plant in the west and is losing us jobs here in Ontario? Is this not simply a case of

February 15, 1990
Oral Questions
a company taking over a Canadian firm, shutting it down, piece by piece, in order to benefit from free trade?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I explained in answer to the hon. member's first question, the company was losing business.
I think the hon. member should be aware of the fact that during the 1980s, on average, 130,000 new corporations were created each year and 100,000 went out of business. Every year four million Canadians change jobs. The hon. member talked about 35 jobs in St. Thomas, and that is regrettable. But I am pleased that Freightlin-er is building a new factory in St. Thomas that will pick up that 35 and about 1,000 more. I think that on balance St. Thomas is well looked after.
The point is that change occurs. The New Democratic Party would like to'stop all change. That is not wise. It is nonsensical.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The February 6, 1990 issue of the Val d'Or L'Echo newspaper referred to a statement made by Mr. Raymond Savoie, the Quebec Minister responsible for mining, and then added:
The minister also confirmed the rumours to the effect that the
PSEC would be phased out by 1991 because of budgetary cuts.
My question is this: Could the minister confirm that Minister Savoie consulted him or his department before announcing that the PSEC for mining exploration would be phased out by 1991 in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot confirm anything relating to either conversations that have been alleged or that might have been mentioned in newspapers, or any speculation on any budgetary matter.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. Yesterday the Economic Council published its report, Good Jobs, Bad Jobs, in which it indicated that 70 per cent of Canadians are now employed in service industries and that there is a growing polarization between the good jobs and bad jobs in this sector, with the result that there is a 'declining middle-class in this country. The report said that this was due to the fact that between 1980 and 1988, half of the jobs created were part-time, temporary, low-paying jobs with low benefits.
When will the government implement the recommendations in this report to better protect these workers and to give them adequate compensation? When are we going to see some action in respect of this report?

Mr. Speaker, I am aware of the report which was tabled yesterday. We have started reviewing it. I am very pleased to inform the hon. member that the Minister of Employment and Immigration in her Labour Force Adjustment Program has forecast $100 million specifically for older workers to get retraining. If his friends in the other Chamber can let Bill C-21 go, we will have $800 million to retrain people in Canada, precisely to occupy these new jobs.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-21 is not doing this in the way in which the Economic Council recommends. If the minister reads the report he will notice that the council states that the growth of these low-paying jobs is undermining the economic security of a significant and growing portion of the workforce. That is an alarming indictment of the government's policies in the employment and labour area.
Will the minister on behalf of the government make a commitment to report soon to this House what the government's response will be to this report, to deal with these workers, the one-half of Canadian workers who are being left out of this growing Canadian economy?
February 15, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell once more to my hon. colleague from Notre-Dame-de-Grace that this government has been involved for many years in setting up programs for preparing Canadian men and women in the labour force to occupy the jobs which exist now or will exist in the future in the new technological industries.
I suggest however that he would do a favour to the Canadian public generally if he managed to convince his non-elected colleagues in the other place to adopt as soon as possible Bill C-21 which is now before the House, thereby making available to us the money we need to provide Canadian men and women with the necessary training to fill up the new jobs of the 1990s and the 2000s.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Over the past few days the minister has been floating trial balloons about possible changes to the ACOA program. The last time the minister took such flights of fancy ACOA suffered a 20 per cent cut and its program criteria was dramatically altered.
Now that the minister has seen the error of his ways, will he give Atlantic Canadians an assurance that his so-called impending changes are not just code words for further gutting of the only regional development program in Atlantic Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I received my colleague's letter yesterday, delivered to my office, in which he earnestly requested to be kept very closely informed about any such changes so that he could adequately respond. I will keep that in mind.
In so far as detrimental effects, I want to point out to the member again that in his constituency alone he has had over 600 jobs created under the auspices of ACOA,
Oral Questions
at estimated total costs of $42 million. I think that perhaps it would be in order for him to wait and see about the changes because ACOA is the best thing he and other members in Atlantic Canada have going.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the minister for his compliment about my competence as the member for Dartmouth.
I would like to read from the Conference Board of Canada report today which states:
The Maritime provinces will have to weather a storm front of
economic uncertainty as major problems in the fisheries adversely
affect their economic performances in 1990 and 1991.
It has been confirmed that a part of the proposed fisheries assistance program will be delivered through the ACOA budget. But what we do not know is how much the program will cost or where the money is going to come from.
Will the minister confirm that any fisheries assistance program will be funded by additional new moneys, or is the minister finally admitting that the promised generous assistance is nothing more than a deceitful reshuffling of an already gutted and battered ACOA budget?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is disappointing to see that my colleague opposite has joined the legion of the perpetually indignant, Mr. Speaker. I can only say to him that the assistance that will be allocated to help the town of Canso and other disadvantaged areas in Atlantic Canada will be real assistance and whether he wants to quibble about old money or new money is up to him.

Mr. Speaker, in a recent article in The Citizen the Canadian Lumbermen's Association president has noted that the jobs hundreds of people across Canada who work at 40 distribution centres for the lumber area where wood is unloaded at warehouses and reloaded in different packages for American customers will be lost as a result of the goods and services tax. They say that to avoid the high cost of financing the tax the reload centres will just simply move across the border.

February 15, 1990
Oral Questions
My question is for the Minister of Finance. Will the minister finally hear the cries of the lumber industry and Canadian workers and finally give the industry and the people of Canada a break?

Mr. Speaker, this is one of those industries that is a major beneficiary of the goods and services tax. The hon. member should realize that included today in the price of fuel, computers and telephones, of building materials, of office equipment, and a range of things are existing federal sales taxes.
As a result of the GST all of that sales tax will be removed from the costs. It will make industries more competitive. It will put them in a better position where that particular industry will be able to sell into their major market, the United States, in a much more competitive way than it can today. That is why the GST is going to create jobs. It will create more wealth for the province of British Columbia. That is why we are in favour of the GST.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that the Minister of Finance thinks that if he continues to tell a lie often enough, or tell his story often enough-
Order!
-that finally the people of Canada will believe that story.
Order.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian lumber industry is still reeling from the 15 per cent tax imposed on it for export to the United States. Will the minister recognize that even this industry does not want the GST? Will he axe the tax now?

Mr. Speaker, I am not sure whether the member from Victoria was distracting you, but when a member says that I have been telling a lie many, many times, then at that stage I draw the line and say no answer to that type of question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I ask the hon. member to withdraw the remark.

Mr. Speaker, I would be most happy to. I tried to
correct the error in my original summation by changing it to story. I am very pleased to withdraw the allegation that there was a lie by the minister. I withdraw that allegation.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence. I would like to ask about the Tracadie at CFB Chatham. For several years now, negotiations have been under way between the federal government and the Province of New Brunswick for additional lands for the Tracadie range associated with CFB Chatham. What is the status of these negotiations at the present time? What will be the extent of the utilization of that land, and what is the environmental impact?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bill McKnight (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member asks several questions. In 1985, the Government of Canada started negotiations with the government of New Brunswick to use New Brunswick Crown land to provide low level air defence training. At the present time those discussions are going forward. At the present time there is a joint environmental impact study being done by the province and the federal government.
The land would be used less than 70 days a year for low level air defence training. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. The minister said recently, and I quote: "-it is not up to the federal

government to be in charge of Montreal's economic recovery; it must come from the community."
Can we conclude that his government accepts the philosophy of the CREESOM report and that the government will financially support RESO, the southwest Montreal local economic development corporation?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to repeat the answer I gave yesterday to a similar question: the CREESOM report was given to us in late December and we then told its authors that we would answer them by late February or early March, and that is what we intend to do in the next few weeks.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's answer is disappointing. He must know that the people of southwest Montreal are eagerly waiting for the government's answer. I am not asking him to give exact figures; I am just asking him to confirm whether he accepts the basic philosophy of the report, which is to encourage community organizations and local solutions, because that seems to tie in with his own philosophy? Yes or no, does he accept this philosophy?

Mr. Speaker, I will repeat it again.

I will repeat it in the other language to make sure that my hon. friend understands. We have said to the authors of this report that we will provide our answer by the end of February or beginning of March, and we intend to respect that deadline.

Now that the Open Skies Conference is over, we have seen the superpowers come to an agreement on troop reductions in Central Europe and we have had a firsthand experience of glasnost internationally, will the

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said at noon at the ceremony on Parliament Hill: In the life of a country, symbols are an important visual manifestation of a nation. They embody a feeling of identity, pride and harmony that transcends all divisions. They are a force that unites citizens as members of one big family.

Today we celebrate perhaps the most visible and beloved symbol of Canada, our national flag. As we mark the twenty-fifth anniversary of the distinctive maple leaf flag we can't help but think back to what we have accomplished together and the heights we have reached since 1965 when the new flag was first raised over Parliament Hill.
The maple leaf flag will always symbolize a united and confident bilingual and multicultural nation at home and around the world.

Today, as we celebrate the historic anniversary of our flag, we celebrate our citizenship and our pride in belonging to a country that we cherish. Canadians from Newfoundland to British Columbia love their country in ways as diverse as their geography and often uniquely personal.
Let us celebrate today the anniversary of this flag that is a matter of personal and common pride, and let us keep building a just and compassionate society that can be a model to the world.

I urge all hon. members to join me in saluting our Canadian flag and the country for which it stands.

subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to thank the new Leader of the Opposition for allowing me to take his place temporarily on this occasion.
Those of us in the Official Opposition who 25 years ago were on the government side and who followed this debate with great diligence cannot but rejoice in today's great celebration.

We all met earlier this morning a lot of young Canadians. They could not believe that we had a debate. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we had a long debate, a very long and very difficult debate. At long last we agreed with each other; agreed to disagree maybe, but at long last we gave Canada and Canadians a new Canadian flag.
A very few days after the debate was over, Canadians from every region and province of the country, as well as people from outside Canada, accepted what is so natural for a country-to have its own symbol.

-a symbol of pride. A symbol of pride is always something that does not denigrate others but gives us who call ourselves Canadians a symbol of our belonging to a country. And that is our flag, the Canadian flag!
On behalf of my party, on behalf of all my colleagues, and on behalf of three members who survived that time, the Right Hon. John N. Turner, the Hon. Herb Gray, our new Opposition Leader, my new Opposition Leader-

On behalf of my new leader and on my own behalf I want to say that it is a great day for us to celebrate 25 years.
We know that 25 years later we are going into some other debate, but we know that people of good faith will find a solution for Canada.
I could not conclude and take my seat without at least giving an extract of a speech that taught me what politicians should be: people of courage. I was very honoured as a young, new parliamentarian to be invited by the right hon. Mr. Pearson to go with him to Winnipeg-yes, Winnipeg-for an address by him as Prime Minister to the Twentieth Dominion Convention
February 15, 1990

of the Royal Canadian Legion at the Capital Theatre on Sunday, May 17, 1964.
It was for me an event that I will never forget. It is a lesson I will teach young Canadians, that when you have strong beliefs you must express them. Mr. Pearson did not choose to go to Quebec City where it would have been very well received and highly popular to say: "We have a new Canadian flag". No, he chose the place where he knew they were the most reluctant.
If you watched TV last night, you will know that he was completely booed by the attendees. I think there was Mrs. Pearson, Mary Macdonald his secretary, myself, and a couple of people somewhere who applauded. You saw that on TV last night. Yet, a few days later he started the debate.
I would like all of us to reflect on this quote in these so-called difficult times that our country is going through on another issue. He said: "We who are elected to serve Canada in Parliament owe all those who elect us more than the advocacy of non-controversial ideas. We owe Canada our best judgment and we fail Canada if we fail to exercise that judgment or if we pass our responsibility for judgment back to the electorate who send us to Parliament."
I would like us to reflect on that. I would like to pay tribute to the right hon. Mr. Pearson and to all those who accepted that it was in the best interest of Canada at that time, since today we all agree that it was the right decision. Young Canadians from all parts of Canada are proud.

Just travel across Canada, in all our provinces, and you will see the pride of our young people when they show they are Canadians by waving the Canadian flag.
Thank you for this occasion! I say to young Canadians: Do not lose hope. We have a great country to build, a country that is growing every day. We will keep building it, but we must not abandon our youth which was our hope, 25 years ago, when we chose this flag.

subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF THE CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today we celebrate together the twenty-fifth anniversary of the raising of the first national flag of Canada, the Canadian maple leaf flag.
As we stood today in front of the Peace Tower in a bitterly cold blizzard, I recalled the tremendous struggles and the many achievements of the people who have gone before us to build this great nation from sea to sea to sea: the aboriginal peoples who have protected this land from its beginnings; the explorers and early settlers in Upper and Lower Canada who spoke English and French; the Fathers of Confederation who met in Charlottetown; the influx of the European immigrants who homesteaded and settled the west; the Chinese workers who built our railroads and the many immigrants who joined them to settle in B.C. Our country and horizons expanded as Newfoundland joined the Canadian family and our appreciation grew with the vast and exciting northern territories.
Many of the pioneers in our history books are men, but the women who also homesteaded raised large families, suffered loneliness and hardship and often died young. They also are the heroines of our history.
My thoughts as we faced the blizzard also went back to my own first experience overseas as a Red Cross worker with Commonwealth forces in Japan and Korea. The maple leaf flag was our rallying point, and we were one Canadian family regardless of our home province or language.
When we travel away from home we realize how fortunate we are to be Canadians and live in a land that is so vast and beautiful and resourceful. We give out our flag pins proudly and usually receive a warm response around the world.
As we stood in the snow today, the hon. Stanley Knowles reminded me of the bitterness and partisanship that preceded the final acceptance of our red maple leaf flag 25 years ago. I could not help but think that watching high over us silently from his permanent place on the Hill was the Leader of the Opposition of that day. I wondered what he was thinking as he looked down on today's proceedings.
Our flag is our symbol of Canada. It symbolizes our love for this beautiful multicultural country and our distinctive Canadian values. We pass on this flag to our

February 15, 1990
Privilege
children to symbolize unity and peace and respect for our varied peoples and varied regions. We want it to fly over a land whose beauty and richness will be protected, to be enjoyed by future generations.

We are Canadians!
